Indeed, people are seen to understand the burning fire from the word "fire" by disregarding the notion of a young boy, but they do not understand the young boy while disregarding the notion of the burning fire.
It is exactly the same in the case of metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā); for one does not understand that which is near the Ganges while disregarding the notion of the Ganges itself.
Therefore, it cannot be said that [the word] is for the purpose of excluding that [secondary sense].

Now, if it is thought that the term "indication" (lakṣaṇā) applies in the case of indication, but does not apply in the case of the secondary sense (gauṇa), that is incorrect. For in terms of cognition, both indeed apply; however, in terms of the result (kārya), not even one of them applies.

Therefore, even by this qualification, no distinction is made. Or, if an effort is made to exclude the meaning of the sentence [as a whole], that is not so; for a sentence does not function toward a different object when its words are expressive of related meanings (*anvitābhidhāyin*).

For a sentence consists of words alone; and the meaning of a sentence is the word-meanings as already connected. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that there is no denotation of unconnected meanings. If this is so, then the sense of the question must be explained. And thus, [the words] are accompanied by their respective suffixes, well-established, and frequently used.
Since this has already been answered in the Bhāṣya, this question intended to refute it is likewise untenable.
It is said: the meaning of this question is as follows: because [the cognition of the sentence-meaning] serves as the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning...

The distinction between word-meanings is understood; and this [distinction] is the same in the case of both "the boy is fire" (*māṇavako ’gniḥ*) and "fire. When it is said "the boy is fire," the boy and his tawny color are the grounds [for the application of the word]. When it is said "fire burns," the burning object and the act of burning are [the grounds]. Therefore, we perceive no difference [between the two cases].

"This is its primary causal status based on verbal expression; this is its secondary causal status. But surely, the cognition of the tawny color in the boy is preceded by the cognition of fire; it cannot be said thus.

To speak on this: it has already been stated that the understanding of a causal basis (*nimittabhāva*) arises from a sentence. In the expression "The fire is the boy" (*agnirmāṇavakaḥ*), it is only the tawny color (*piṅgalatā*) that is understood as the causal basis, just as in the expression "The tawny boy. Therefore, the distinction between "this is secondary" (*gauṇa*) and "this is primary" (*mukhya*) is difficult to define; so [the opponent] thinks.

This is not a question; furthermore, it has been demonstrated in the Bhāṣya that this cannot be established by means of *upapada* (governing words) and so forth. In the case of "this boy is like fire" (*agnir ivāyaṃ māṇavakaḥ*), it is appropriate for *iva* and other such particles to be employed in the sense of similarity, as there is a similarity with fire.

Because it is seen [in usage]. However, in the case of "The boy is fire" (*agnir māṇavakaḥ*), the meaning of the sentence is devoid of the sense of "as if" (*iva*); and just as in "The boy is tawny" (*piṅgalo māṇavakaḥ*), the status of being the cause [for the application of the word] is the same. Therefore, we consider this section to be entirely purposeless. How then [do you explain] "A hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) or "Gargas at the well" (*kūpe gargāḥ*)?

Regarding the word "family" (*kula*): it is not possible for the force of the expression "he dwells in" (*prativasati*) to apply [directly], so it is connected with proximity. However, in the case of "The boy is fire" (*agnir māṇavakaḥ*), the comprehension of the quality of being tawny (*piṅgala-guṇa*) would not be established in any way [if taken literally].
Therefore, let there be *lakṣaṇā* (indication). But in the case of *gauṇatva* (secondary or metaphorical usage), there is nothing [to be gained].

There is a means of valid cognition [for this]. And how is it that in the world the cognition of fire arises even from its tawny color, just as the cognition of "other" arises from "prior" and so forth? To this it is replied: this cognition is based solely on the sense of "as it were" (iva).
Why? Because it is understood in that way. But how can the sense of "as if" (iva) be perceived without the word *iva*?

Why even postulate the sense of "as if" when the word *iva* itself is absent? If you say it is because we observe its usage [in such cases], then the same applies here as well. [Objection: But surely, once the tawny color (*paiṅgalya*) is understood, the similarity to fire is understood; [it is] not otherwise.

It was stated that it is "like sound. This is not tenable; for then there would also be the cognition, "Fire is like a young brahmin boy," whereas here the case is the opposite. Because of its extreme redness, the flame—

If it is argued that there is no analogy [for this], we reply that there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for such a conception. It is logical to postulate a cause according to how it is understood, because the understanding of the cause is rooted in that [analogy].
Therefore, although the opposite might be possible, it does not gain a foothold because it contradicts what is well-established.

For origination (*saṃbhava*) has no counter-position; therefore, it is logical that there is both a primary and a secondary designation based on the application (*prayoga*) and the causal condition (*pratyaya*). Is the application of the mantras restricted solely to the primary denotation, or does it extend to the secondary as well? Therefore, this investigation is appropriate.

What, then, is the prima facie position? Since there is no distinction, both are denoted; for the usage "the fire blazes" is observed, as is the usage "the boy is fire. Therefore, there is no decisive criterion [for determining one over the other].

There is a reason for this. To this it is replied: it has been demonstrated that while there is no primary denotation devoid of [an object], there is secondary denotation. Therefore, the function of a word is indeed primary. Mantras assist through denotation, and denotation applies to the primary [meaning].

It does not apply in a secondary sense. From what, then, does the secondary cognition arise? It arises from similarity. This is true as you have said, but that [similarity] is mentioned as a means (*upāya*), and not for the purpose of negating the primary cause.
And by whom was it said that the status of being a cause is negated? [The rule applies] when the primary sense is possible.

It is merely stated that application to a secondary sense is not permissible; however, where it is impossible in the primary sense, recourse to a secondary sense is indeed accepted as a means. In that case, there would be no displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *anumantraṇas* for Pūṣan and others, since they have been applied by means of their respective names (*samākhyā*).

The excellence lies in the fact that it is possible only in the primary sense. Therefore, where there is comprehension of the primary sense, there is no authority for the restriction of the mantra even in the secondary sense. Why does it cause the primary sense to be understood? It is simply because—
This has been demonstrated by Mādhava:
"But because of the scriptural statement, the Aindrī [verse] would be used even if it does not correspond to the actual fact. (Sūtra 3.2.3).

Regarding the injunction, "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindra mantra," there arises a doubt: does the Aindra mantra denote the Gārhapatya fire, or does it denote Indra? But how can there be a doubt when the scriptural statement "one worships the Gārhapatya" is so explicit? [The answer is: because a mantra is to be employed according to its primary meaning.
It is established in the preceding section. But surely, even when the primary sense is impossible, it is indeed applied in a secondary sense.
We simply do not know whether such a possibility exists or not.
[Is it not so that] "he worships the Gārhapatya fire" is a clear scriptural injunction (*śruti*)? [This depends on] the capacity of that which is to be applied...

We say that the second case ending occurs for an unintended object when it is used in the sense of *sārī* (a byproduct). And so it is recorded in the traditional rule: "Likewise, that which is joined [with the action] but is not intended (*anīpsita*) [is also called *karman*]."
Thus [it is said]. And this very [mantra] is its subject matter;

by virtue of what is to be employed, it culminates in a *kāraka* (grammatical factor). Alternatively, since one approaches the *gārhapatya* fire and then addresses [it], the use of the accusative case is indeed appropriate. Therefore, it is an address to Indra. And this is precisely correct.

Otherwise, a non-worldly (alaukikī) denotative power (*abhidhānaśakti*) would have to be postulated. [Objection: But surely there will be a figurative denotation (*gauṇamabhidhānam*). [Reply: There is no such thing as figurative denotation. For figurative denotation occurs when usage is already established;
it is not the case that usage is established on the basis of figurative denotation. And in this case, there is no usage of the word "Indra" with respect to the *gārhapatya* fire.

The accomplishment [of the application] arises from the instruction regarding what is to be done; therefore, the application follows the designation. This is stated here: the designation "gārhapatya" must be performed by means of the mantra. Why?
Because the action must be performed according to the instruction, and the instruction does not follow the action; for that [instruction] is an extended application (*atideśa*).

But has it not been stated in the first section of the seventh book that the instruction is also according to the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished)? In that context, the word *kārya* was used to denote the meaning of *niyoga* (an injunction), and not attainment (*āpti*) and so forth. But surely, it is precisely in the matter of application (*viniyoga*)...

It was stated that "it is doubted. If one asks why it is not certain, [the answer is] because the accusative case is seen even in the case of what is not intended (*anīpsita*). What, then, is this "not intended"? It is that which is "connected in such a way and not intended" (*tathā yuktam cānīpsitam*). In that case, the primary status (*prādhānya*) with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is all the more evident; for otherwise, [this would not be possible].

In that case, such a connection would not be possible. If so, for what purpose is the suffix *tara* used here? It is to indicate that even that which is not desired [by the agent] may be the primary factor.

But was it not said that the power of a word cannot be postulated if it has not been perceived? What here is unperceived? From the statement itself, it is indeed perceived. It is not possible to understand the power of word-meanings from the statement alone. How then [is it understood] in the case of the accomplishment of the meaning of an injunction through connection (*yoga*) and so forth?

[Objection: Is it not a capacity (*śakti*)? [Reply: Because [capacity] is understood through its effect (*kārya*). But here, the case is the opposite. If there were a statement here that "it is to be understood," then there would be the observation of an effect. However, this statement—"With the *aindrī* [verse], one worships the *gārhapatya* fire"—is intended for something else entirely. This has been stated as a "connection" (*sambandha*).

"Because it is the cause of the treatise. [Objection: Then the designation must be figurative. [Reply: But was it not already stated that a designation is figurative when the practical application is established? Here too, the effect—[p. b720]
"Therefore, he is perfected; thus there is no distinction. Considering that the mention of qualities in the Sūtra is for the sake of illustration, the Commentator stated, "and from yoga.
[Objection: "If it is argued that the same applies to rising [from the body] as well... (Sūtra 3.2.5). Section 3.2.5.1.3.
In this case as well, the meaning of "he threshes while calling" is that one should perform the threshing by means of the calling;
or rather, the naming [of the act] will occur through a secondary quality (guṇa) or through etymological connection (yoga), such that "he calls" (*āhvayati*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). For he who—

By saying "hi," he indeed issues an invitation. As for how it is "three times": because of the reading in another recension (śākhā), this "three times" is also merely a restatement (anuvāda). To this, it is replied: only "three times" is prescribed here.

Everything else is restated. Now, one might object that "three times" is also already established; but no, because there is no fixed rule, as it is recited twice in some instances. Therefore, the phrase "while threshing" is a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). This is not a fault, because [the action] is obtained from another source. Now, one might object that since the threshing has already commenced, this mantra would not apply; but this too is obtained from another source.
Since it is already established, this objection is not to be raised. Therefore, there is no authority for a figurative application.
Furthermore, if this mantra were to have its primary meaning in the act of threshing, then a secondary metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would not need to be assumed for the act of threshing.
It might be so; and it is possible to denote threshing by the word *haviṣkṛt*, just as [the word] denotes the wife (*patnī*). True, it is possible;

however, the invocation would then result in an incoherent meaning, and the number "three" would become indefinite. Therefore, it is better to take it as a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And by that, the gender—
[The rule] concerning radiance;
likewise [the rules] regarding rising and dismissal. (3-2-10, Section 4)
But surely this is merely an illustrative example; what is being extended here? For similarity is not possible apart from difference. This difference exists in the preceding section (p.

"Three times"—this alone is enjoined; everything else is restated. However, in this case, a connection with time must be enjoined. Since such a connection was not previously established, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers it improper to employ figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when enjoining that which was not already obtained; thus he perceives a difference between this case and the preceding topic. The proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*), however, [responds] because this is equal to the case where the meaning of the command (*praiṣa*) lacks syntactic connection.
He said, "So be it.
And [the rule regarding] time in the *sūktavāka* is for the sake of another, because it serves a different purpose. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.2.11, Adhikaraṇa 5).

To this it is replied: this is not a definition of time; what then? This is an instruction regarding a mantra. But was it not stated that a mantra has another purpose and does not denote the act of taking away (*harati*)?

Let it not be that [the word] *harati* is a denoter of the act of taking; rather, it will be a denoter of the deity who takes. But surely this [word] denotes a deity for whom the sacrifice has already been completed (*nirvṛtta-yāga*). And *harati* is not the same as *yajati* (to sacrifice). It is said in reply:

even though it denotes a deity for whom the sacrifice has been completed, there will be a sacrifice that serves as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for that [deity], just like the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
But has it not been stated that this is the root *harati* (to take), not *yajati* (to sacrifice)? The root *harati* is indeed *yajati*, because of its connection with the mantra.
But if that is the case, does it not follow that there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? It is not a figurative indication, because it refers to the sacrifice.

Because the object of "being" (*sati*) is already established, it functions as a subordinate element, just like the verb *ālabheta* ("one should immolate"). Otherwise, this would have to be indicated as a completed action (*vṛttam*). Furthermore, the expression *āśāste* ("he desires") is an indication of a state already accomplished (*bhūta-nirdeśa*).

Therefore, it is well said that *harati* (he takes away) is synonymous with *yajati* (he sacrifices). As for what was stated—that when there is a disposal (*pratipatti*), it is not logical for it to be a purposeful act (*arthakarma*)—it has been replied that there will be no contradiction, as in the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
Sūtra 3.2.16: "Because of the instruction regarding the whole, the term 'all' applies to both cases. (A. 6)

It has been established that the *harati*, the *yajati*, and the *sūktavāka* mantra [are distinct]. Now this is considered: is the entire *sūktavāka* to be employed on both the full moon and the new moon days, or is it according to the division of the words for the deities?

But surely this very reflection is untenable. It has been established that there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) because of the unity of meaning; however, in the case of principal deity-words that are recited in a joined manner (*śliṣṭapaṭhita*), neither a single meaning nor mutual expectancy upon being divided is possible here.

Therefore, these are distinct. But when there is a singular designation for things that are distinct, how can the performance of the whole be suspected? Just as when it is said "the Āgneyī," it does not mean all the Āgneyīs.

The doubt arises that [the mantra] should be employed [in this way]. Furthermore, it is an established principle that when a primary application is possible, there is no application in a secondary sense. It is replied: as you have said; however, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that the *sūktavāka* exists within a collection of sentences (*vākyasamūha*).
This statement is likewise applicable here: by the phrase "with the *sūktavāka*," this singular number refers to the collection as a whole;
therefore, it is the aggregate itself that serves as the instrument here.

But surely, it may be argued, a single purpose for a collection is not possible; it must be inferred from a scriptural statement, as in the case of the *uttama-prayāja*. To dispel this doubt, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is undertaken. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been established. Now, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is stated: there is no application of the collection here.

There is no authoritative evidence that "the *sūktavāka* exists," because the use of the singular number is possible even otherwise. For it is appropriate for the reciters to use the designation "the *sūktavāka* exists" because it expresses a single [textual] entity. However, in this case—[in the injunction] "one offers the grass-bundle (*prastara*) with the *sūktavāka*"—it is not possible to establish syntactic unity by overriding the gender [of the word].
It cannot be so imagined, because application according to the respective indicative marks (*liṅga*) is logically established. Therefore, since no distinction is perceived,
by whichever *sūktavāka* one offers the grass-bundle (*prastara*), it becomes offered by means of the *sūktavāka*.
"He strikes" is stated with reference to the collective whole as that which is to be abandoned.
"On account of the indicative mark, the order, and the name, the recitation is connected with the optional rites. (JS 2.3.7)

In the preceding section, it was stated that when there is a possibility of each [subsidiary] being subsidiary by virtue of context (*prakaraṇa*), the division is determined by indicative mark (*liṅga*). Now, here the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that whatever is stronger than context is all the more powerful than both order (*krama*) and name (*samākhyā*); for when subsidiariness is established by indicative mark, the other factors are not independent.
Regarding the two named "Order" (krama) and "Name" (samākhyā):

indeed, it will be stated in the final conclusion (rāddhānta) that indicative mark (liṅga) alone is not the applicator; rather, it is in its capacity as an applicator that its relative strength or weakness [is determined].

[Page b730] For what purpose, then, is there an investigation into relative strength prior to the section on *śruti* (direct statement) and *liṅga* (indicative power)? To this it is replied: This is not an investigation into relative strength at all; rather, it concerns *liṅga* as being dependent [on other factors].
It is established here that [the word] is "that which enjoins. How, then, is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) formulated?

This is the prima facie view because of its inclusion in the Sūtra on relative strength (*balābala-sūtra*), which states that even an indicative mark (*liṅga*)—like direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth—is independent of other means of knowledge. However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: when a general connection exists...

The indicative mark (*liṅga*) is the means of application regarding the specific [function] of the remainder. Just as the indicative mark is not the sole means of application, we shall demonstrate this more thoroughly in the section on *Śruti* and *Liṅga*. Therefore, the indicative mark, when accompanied by the order of sequence (*krama*), is the means of application.
And the purpose for the combination of both types of evidence (linga and pramāṇa) has been stated in the Bhāṣya:
"In the case of eligibility, there is an injunction regarding mantras because they are taught among those that are not otherwise explained. (JS 3.2.8)

Regarding such indications of gender as "One should stand near the Āgnīdhra fire-altar with a verse addressed to Agni" (āgneyyā), should all [verses] possessing that gender be taken, or is there to be the inclusion of only those [verses] under discussion in the context? This is the position of the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī).

However, thinking that the capacity of the term to denote the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛta*) is not possible for that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), he says, "the taking up [of the vessel] lasts as long as the sign (*liṅga*). For the word denoting the subject (*uddeśyapada*) depends upon the subject matter under discussion, but it does not also serve to present the meaning of the thing to be enjoined. Indeed, being the subject (*uddeśyatva*) consists in having a purposeful meaning. And...

A universal (*sāmānya*) becomes purposeful because its object is grasped, for purposefulness consists in the grasping [of an object]. But is it not the case that the universal itself is what is grasped? No, for the grasping of an unlimited [universal] is impossible.

Therefore, in that context, the universal exists only as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). As it was stated in the section on the cups (*grahādhikaraṇa*): "Furthermore, that which is to be enjoined..."
The number is to be understood from the word itself, because it cannot be known from any other source; this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Whether the primary or the secondary [element], as many as there are indicators (*liṅga*), are to be enjoined. Is it by means of the primary elements that they possess the indicators?

"Should one attend to [the mantras] possessing such characteristics, or should one bring in from the *Daśatayīs* those that possess such characteristics?"—thus, the mention of the *Daśatayīs* is not intended as an alternative to the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*).

What is meant is this: "Are all those possessing such characteristics to be taken, or should only those possessing such characteristics that are already present in the context (*prakṛta*) be brought in?"
Thus [it is asked]:
"Is this—that which has already been taught being taught again—not improper?
This is this: that which has been taught—

For that alone is its distinction; and it has been stated that this [distinction] is not a constituent part of the injunction (*vidheya*). However, the status as the subject matter (*prakṛtatva*) is equal because of being mentioned again. To this, he says: when there is a conflict, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is sublated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*).

"And there is no contradiction between these two. What is the intended meaning? This is the intended meaning: even when the primary substance (prakṛta) is being taken up, the very purpose already expressed becomes fulfilled. Just as when a single cow is being employed, the Vedic injunction "one should sacrifice a cow" has its purpose accomplished. [Objection: It is not so. [Response: Not so here.

It is held that "possessing the indicative mark" (*liṅgavattā*) is the meaning of the word. It is replied: this presentation of the position is for the purpose of its rejection, on the grounds that "it possesses that mark by means of this. Furthermore, since the context concerns a specific manifestation of a mantra within the *Dāśatayī*, the sublation of the contextual [meaning]—when the meaning of the indicative mark has already been established—is without any basis of proof.
One thinks:
"But some cognition produced by a logical mark (liṅga) is false."

When the meaning of the indicative mark (liṅga) is fully established, what is this state of falsity? The intended meaning is this: it is not the case that this general application (sāmānyopasaṃhāra) is the word-meaning [itself], as in the injunction, “One desiring heaven should sacrifice.”

Thus, it cannot be said that the meaning of the treatise is concluded by the actual performance [of the rite], even if it is fit for another application. Now, one might object: "Since the individual is not the meaning of the word, only the subsumption under the universal has been presented. This very point we do not understand.

Thus, because the meaning of the suffix is primary in the case of words ending in *taddhita* suffixes, it is considered that their possession of that quality (*tadvattā*) is not a constituent part (*aṅga*).
Therefore, this treatise is not intended for the purpose of formulating a general rule. But has this not already been stated?

This presentation is made in order to avoid the charge of "teaching what has already been taught" (*upadiṣṭopadeśa*), on the grounds that the instruction regarding the subject at hand in one context does not mean it will be taught as a different matter in another. Why is this so? Because it has been shown that [the word] refers merely to that which possesses the characteristic mark (*liṅgavat*). In this case, the fact of having been previously taught is not the reason. But is it not thus...?
If it exists, there is sublation of the context (*prakṛta*). Let there be sublation of the context due to its being directly expressed; that is not a fault.
Moreover, neither the indicative mark (*liṅga*) nor the context (*prakaraṇa*) is something that must be favored; therefore, it is not for the sake of favoring them [that the sublation occurs].

This is that which was stated as "the summary of the meaning of the treatise": "Or [the name of the Veda] is that [of its author], because of both the context and the logical possibility. (3.1.22) Sūtra 8.

To this it is replied: the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), however, considering that even in the present case a suffix denoting something to be enjoined (vidheya) is not at all impossible, stated that the reference must be to the subject matter at hand (prakṛta). How so? For being the "subject of an injunction" (uddeśyatva) belongs only to that which possesses a purpose.

Furthermore, the fact that something is the subject under discussion does not at all obstruct the application of a term denoting the subject to that which is to be enjoined; for when a specific instance is present, a general term does not bypass it, just as in the case of "blue lotus."
Or it is like [the command] "bring the cow. Therefore, the word must not be a general term referring to the subject at hand;
rather, it is established that only those specific genders and individuals under discussion are intended.
And because all [of them] have been taught—this refers to what was stated: if there is merely an instruction in every case...
It has been stated that even when the context is taken into account, the direct instruction (*upadeśa*) is not a qualifier.
[Sūtra 3.1.25] "By means of indicative mark (*liṅga*) and name (*samākhyā*), the section belongs to the purpose of eating. (A. 9)

Now this is considered: just as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been concluded on the basis of its being the subject at hand, does the name (*samākhyā*) also conclude itself solely on the basis of its own cause, or is its application according to the indicative mark?
What, then, is reasonable? That the name also restricts [the application] just like the subject at hand.

The indicative mark (*liṅga*) [indicates] a specific [meaning]. Now, an objection: does this not result in a contradiction with other indicative marks? No, because there is no contradiction with other indicative marks even when [the word] functions as a qualifier. For whether it denotes its own meaning or the meaning of another, the act of denotation is indistinguishable. But surely, if it denotes the meaning of another, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would result? Even so—
The designation is not distinct; this is a distinction in its intent toward this specific purpose, not a distinction in the designation itself.
Therefore, the name is capable of being restrictive.
1. There is a reduction [of the meaning] because of the teaching of its form and because the purpose has been enjoined. (3.2.16)

It is true that there is another indicative mark (liṅga) which is not contradictory; however, there is no evidence for it not having as its primary purpose something other than this [the ritual]. For even the object of another indicative mark, such as eating, is worthy of being remembered; indeed, the application (prayoga) is what must be remembered, and the taking up [of the vessel] and so forth are themselves the application.

Therefore, the application is established according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*). But is it not the case that an indicative mark devoid of a name (*samākhyā*) does not even attain the capacity to apply? It is certainly not devoid of a name;
