To this it is replied: it is not so; for "he offers" (*juhoti*) and "sacrifice" (*yajati*) [are distinct].
These are to be accomplished by means of substances belonging to one's relatives. Furthermore, if there were a complete renunciation of everything,
the oblation (*homa*) and sacrifices such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* would not be possible.
The injunctions concerning the *aṣṭākapāla* (the cake on eight potsherds) are thus established. Therefore, a doubt arises.

And in this doubt, which side’s position is it proper to adopt? First, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that because the injunction for the *āgneya* [offering] has no counter-injunction and because [the subsequent injunctions] depend upon it—
The former *rāsa* alone is more powerful; thus it has been said: "There is an offering of the whole oblation, because that is its purpose.
How then is it that one says, "He offers the fourfold portion," and [offers] to the *sviṣṭakṛt*?

"He cuts off" (*avadyati*). Either the meaning of *yajati* (sacrifices) and *juhoti* (offers) must be understood here in a figurative sense, or another substance possessing those characteristics must be produced. "He cuts off twice from the oblation" means he cuts off from that which possesses the characteristics of an oblation.
However, because the ritual action has already been performed, it should be done only once, since the substance is subordinate to the action. (3.4.40)

To this it is replied: It is indeed true as you have stated, provided that the taddhita suffix in the expression "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ) were to extend up to the act of relinquishment (tyāga).

Since it is understood that "this is its deity" merely as a general relation, the state of being related is indeed possible even through the abandonment of one part. This is what was stated: "The formation of a secondary derivative (taddhita) is possible even when the relation is incomplete; therefore, it should be understood that the connection [is established] by what has been shown."

And this being the case, once the injunction for the Āgneya offering has been established, it is possible to assume a figurative application (gauṇī vṛtti) for the statements, "He offers the fourfold portion" and "He cuts off [the portion] for the Sviṣṭakṛt. Or rather, [it refers to] the substance which possesses the characteristics of the oblation-material.

Thus, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by the four-fold cutting alone; consequently, the observation of [rites such as] the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering for the cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni becomes logical. As for the further doubt raised—that because the two-fold cutting is a preparatory act (*saṃskāra*), there is no contradiction in discarding the entire [cake]—that very doubt...
It has been stated that the measure alone constitutes the oblation, because it serves the purpose of the sacrifice.
b849] || 15 || Because they are not the motive, the [portions] should be prepared from a single [animal], since the remainder is subordinate. || 42 ||

In this regard, the remaining rites serve as the illustration: should one stop after performing them once, or should there be repetition as long as the remainder exists? The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that since the purpose of the scripture has been accomplished, they should be performed only once. [Objection: But surely, as a rule, subordinate elements (*guṇa*) are repeated for each primary element (*pradhāna*); thus, regarding the remainder—
In this context, repetition (*āvṛtti*) is understood as if it were primary. This is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*):

since the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) is for the sake of assisting the principal (*pradhāna*), and since the purpose is accomplished by performing it once, he does not consider repetition to be necessary. For being a subordinate element does not imply that it must be refined [repeatedly]. But surely...
The same would apply even in the case of the *graha* (cup) and so forth. It would indeed apply if this were not resolved here.
In that case, what is there to consider? It has been stated that singularity is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣā*).

To this, it is replied: repetition continues as long as there is a remainder. But was it not said that because the purpose of the scriptural injunction has already been fulfilled, it should be performed only once?
It is said:
For it has been stated that the status of being assisted by the principal act occurs through the medium of the remaining *saṃskāras*.
And no distinction is perceived among those remainders—such as "this one," "that one," or "the other. Therefore, since they are not being specifically apprehended...
Because of the distinction, there is a repetition for each primary act, and the indicative marks have been shown in the Bhāṣya.

As for the prima facie view that "because the subsidiaries lack a purpose," this is precisely what is meant by the statement that they do not possess the status of being objects of refinement (*saṃskārya*) due to being subsidiaries; it does not, however, mean that one considers the subsidiary to be a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*). For indeed—
The status of the remainder as being either a motivator (*prayojaka*) or a non-motivator (*aprayojaka*) is thus established. Therefore, that alone is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
|| 16 || If [the result] were from one [action], there would be no restriction regarding the objects of desire, because there is no distinction. || 46 ||

In the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the preceding section, this consideration concerns the performance of the rite. Here, the prima facie view is that, since there is no specific distinction, it may be performed from any source whatsoever.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that as long as the primary cause (*mukhya-nimitta*) remains intact, it is impossible to effect the destruction of the contingent ritual (*naimittika-upaghāta*). However, since the secondary elements have already been performed, it is indeed proper not to perform the remaining contingent rites once the perception of the [primary] cause has ceased. Thus.
17. Because no mention is made of eating, the word "giving" (dāna) refers to a purchase (parikraya).

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that the purchase [of the officiating priests] is performed with the remnants of the sacrifice, based on the passage "This is for Brahman," which involves the taking up of two portions. However, the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*) maintains that since it is produced precisely as something fit to be cut off, it serves solely the purpose of the sacrifice and thus cannot be employed for any other purpose. If so, how then [is the purchase performed]?
The sacrifice beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* is possible because the remnant has not been relinquished and because of a scriptural injunction.
But surely, the giving away [of the remnant] will also occur by virtue of an injunction? True—if there were such an injunction.

However, in this context, it is heard that [the act] is a gift (*dāna*); yet, since the scriptural statement regarding its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) is also logically consistent with its being a benefit (*upakāra*), the benefit has been demonstrated. It is undeniable, however, that the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣabhāva*) is precisely the opposite.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the *Bṛhatī*.
The fifth quarter of the third chapter.
And because of the ghee, [the rule applies] to all combinations. 3-5-1.
It has been established that one should take the *avatta* (portion) from all the remaining oblation (*havir*) whatsoever that has been prescribed.

Regarding the *upāṃśuyāja*, there is a doubt: should the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering be made from the portion taken from the *dhruvā* vessel—which is common to both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*)—or should it be made from the portion of the primary sacrifice itself, even though it also includes the remnants of the subsidiaries? Which [of these] should be taken?

[The rule] regarding the two portions from the *jauhvā* [ladle] is like that of the *camasa* cups. Since there is no distinction, it might be argued that one should take [the portion] from the common [oblation]. But this is not so;

for in the case of what is common, there is an absence of "remainder-ness" (*śeṣatva*). Indeed, even that which remains is still common to all. Furthermore, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is an extraction from the remainder of the principal sacrifice (*pradhāna*), and it cannot be said that it is the remainder of the principal sacrifice alone.
Precisely because it is common to all; as for the argument that what has been taken up must be consumed, like the cup (*camasa*),
that is incorrect, because of the scriptural injunction "one offers the fourfold portion," which leaves no authority for leaving a remnant.

If it is argued that the injunction regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* portioning is itself the authority, we say no; for it is meaningful even when the remnant (*śeṣa*) has not been employed [in the primary sacrifice]. As for what was said regarding the analogy with the *camasa* cups, that is not correct, because the scriptural mention of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* has no other scope [than the specific context]. [Therefore, there is no *sviṣṭakṛt* portioning, nor is that [remnant] a remnant of the principal offering.]
It can be said that because the *camasa* (cup) is heard [in the text] merely as something to be taken up, the [objection regarding its] observation has been refuted.
|| 2 || In the *Sākaṃprasthāyya* sacrifice, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* are likewise [to be performed]. || 13 ||
By what distinction is this extension (atideśa) made? Since the rule "as in the archetype" (prakṛtivat) applies,
the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers the remainder to be for the sake of the ritual action.
The established conclusion is that the purpose (kārya) prevails because of the scriptural statement.
And [this applies] to the cups (graha) in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice as well. || 3 || 14 ||

In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, because of the statement, “He leaves a remnant; he does not offer it as a complete oblation,” the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) again suspects that there is a remainder and considers the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering to be required. This [is argued] elsewhere regarding that [sacrifice].
The established conclusion is that [the rites] are performed because of their specific application (viniyoga).
|| 4 || When there is a single substance, they should be performed for each individual action due to the difference between the actions. || 16 ||
However, in the case of "sarvapṛṣṭha," one considers there to be a repetition of the remaining purificatory rites and so forth for each primary offering (*pratipradhānam*).
This is the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*): that the meaning of the scripture is determined by the fact that no specific distinction is perceived. But surely—

It has been stated that there is no *sviṣṭakṛt* offering at all in the case of what is common [to both]. True; however, the distinction lies in the fact that other ritual functions have not been performed and because of the relative predominance of the subordinate and the principal elements.
|| 35 || But in the case of the cup for Indra and Vāyu, there shall be a consumption [of the remnant] for each individual action, because of a specific scriptural injunction. || 18 ||

But surely, there is no prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) here at all because of the scriptural statement; for it cannot be said that the statement has another purpose in the context of the prima facie argument. To this it is replied: this is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view—that [the statement] is for the sake of the consecration of the Soma.
The statement "twice of the *bhakṣa*" will be a restatement (*anuvāda*) with reference to another application.
However, the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntavādī*) stated that "the ritual action is to be inferred from the scriptural injunction," because it is based on the injunction.
6. In some cases, because there is no scriptural injunction, eating [the sacrificial food] does not take place. 19.

There is a doubt as to whether or not there is a remnant (*śeṣa*) to be consumed. Now, is it not improper for this doubt to arise, since the Soma is indeed a remnant? It is appropriate [to speak of a remnant] in the case of the *puroḍāśa* and other offerings, because of the scriptural statement, "He cuts off twice from the oblation," whereby the sacrifice is concluded with that portion, and thus those materials possess the status of being remnants.

And for that [cup], there is a consumption [of the remnant]; but here, because of its absence, there is no suspicion of consumption at all. How then are these statements to be understood: “He consumes the Aindravāyava cup twice,” and “Having carried it around on all sides” [etc.]?
And regarding [the rule] "he pronounces the secondary vaṣaṭ-call after the Śvitra," you yourself must be questioned on this point as well: now...
Or let them be purposeful actions (*arthakarman*). How then [do we explain] the expressions "of the Aindravāyava" and "the Āśvina"?

That will be for the purpose of indicating the characteristics of those [portions]. Therefore, it is simply untenable to ask whether or not there exists a consumption of the *soma* remnant. Furthermore, if it is postulated on the basis of these very statements that "the remnant must be set aside," no; for the remnants lack a motivating purpose (*aprayojakatva*). For that which is to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*) is the primary element.
It is an act of consecration (*saṃskārakarma*), and one does not employ that which is not primary. Therefore, the underlying principle (*nyāya*) in this matter must be stated.

It is said: there is no authority for an offering of the entire [substance] here. For in the case of the cups for Indra-Vāyu and others, the drawing [of the juice] is for the sake of those deities; once even a single portion of what has been drawn has been offered, the requirement for the cup dedicated to Indra-Vāyu is indeed fulfilled.
Why is there an offering of the whole? Is it not the case that the entire substance is heard in scripture to be for the purpose of sacrifice, as in "One should sacrifice with soma"?
Even there, it is established that [the sacrifice is performed] by means of only a portion of the soma. Likewise...
And there is the taking of this [portion] and the discarding of the *ṛjīṣa* and so forth. If that is so, why does the text say, "He takes two portions from the sacrificial oblation"?

The conclusion follows from this very point alone, since the application [of the rule] is established there in whatever way possible. If it is argued that this is for the sake of restriction, then the opponent's position—that the entire substance is to be offered—would not be tenable;
moreover, since it is possible even with a single part, one cannot conclude that the whole must necessarily be offered.
This is indeed possible even through an offering of the whole. Therefore, a distinction must be stated.

This is now explained: once the purpose of the scripture has been accomplished, there is no further performance. It has already been demonstrated that the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by means of a single part. How, then, can there be a doubt regarding the offering of the whole?

Because one understands the meaning of the statement that "it should be given after being repeatedly divided," the conclusion is not that the substance exists for the sake of the sacrifice; therefore, this is indeed a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding a single portion.

For this very reason, worldly people prepare milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other offerings for a deity, and having set aside a portion from it for the deity, they employ the remainder as they please. Therefore, a doubt arises: is the disposal of the remnant accomplished solely by eating it, or not? [This is] because of the scriptural injunction...

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that [the eating] does not occur because of the existence [of the rule], since there is no injunction for eating. The second view is that it does exist, because of the injunction of a specific [form of] eating;

for otherwise, the injunction of a specific detail would be untenable. If the injunction of a specific detail is untenable, let it be so; however, eating cannot be established without a scriptural statement (*vacana*).

When one eats, then [the mantra is recited] twice; for it is established in this very way. If that is so, then the conclusion (rāddhānta) is that these are indeed distinct utterances, because each utterance is as much as the specific word itself.
||7|| [The cups] are for the Camasins, because of the designation [of the cups by their names], since the connection [between the cup and the person] is based on that [designation]. || 22 ||

The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that [the term] does not apply to the *camasas* now, because there is no scriptural statement to that effect. However, its status as a *camasa* would otherwise be untenable; for just as in the previous case, the specific injunction "this is his *camasa*" would otherwise be inexplicable. Furthermore, the drinking from another substance, such as carving and so forth, [would likewise be inconsistent].
And it has been demonstrated that [the word "udgātṛ"] does not admit of figurative interpretation. || 8 || [The cup] belongs to one [priest], because of its connection with the Vedic text. || 8 ||
Regarding the phrase "of those who sing" (*prodgātṛṇām*), what is the reason that it does not indicate singing (*gāna*)?
Why does the name (*samākhyā*) alone indicate it? It follows that the word *ud* would be unintended (*avivakṣā*) with respect to those who perform the singing.
When they are being observed, it is shown as follows: "Singing (gāna) is one thing, and chanting (udgāna) is another.

However, this fault does not apply in the case of a conventional designation (samākhyāna). Now, one might object: "But there is no such thing as 'chanting' (udgāna) that is distinct from 'singing' (gāna)."

For that [sāman] is indeed *bhakti* (a part). And that is what is denoted by the term *udgītha*. Furthermore, regarding such usages as "one who should sing the *udgītha*" (*yaḥ punarudgāyet*), the meaning is "one should sing the *udgītha-bhakti*. For in that context, the prefix *ut-* has the sense of indicating the *bhakti*, while the act of singing (*gāna*) remains simply singing (*gāna*). Therefore, [the term] *udgātṛ*...

This is merely a specific name for an officiant (*ṛtvij*); it does not mean that the "Udgātṛ" is the performer of the act of singing (*udgāna*). For this very reason, it was established as the final conclusion (*rāddhāntita*) that in this case, the conventional designation (*samākhyā*) alone is capable of indicating [the agent], and not the act of singing itself.
Therefore, even those who argue against the *Subrahmaṇyā* formula are indeed proponents of an improper argument; it is not the case here that...

[Page b864] There exists no restrictive authority such as the hearing of praise and so forth. Now, one might ask: since the plural number in the phrase "of the *udgātṛ*s" is appropriate for exactly three, why is it that the consumption belongs to the *brahman* priest together with them?
If it is true that the plural number is for the sake of logical consistency, it has been stated here that the word *udgātṛ* refers to those who perform its function.
|| 9 || There is no portion for the *grāvastut* because it is not mentioned [in the text]. || 27 ||

It has been stated that the consumption [of the soma] is established both by direct statement (*vacana*) and by designation (*samākhyāna*). Now, these sections are commenced for the purpose of reaching a consensus regarding disagreements concerning the meaning of those statements. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that "all [the priests] should desire [to consume] at the end of the *hāriyojana* cup," and thus it belongs to the *camasins* alone.

The proponent raises an objection: [This is so] because of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). Since the word "all" refers to the subject at hand and is therefore not ambiguous, it is not appropriate to restrict its scope based on the remainder of the sentence; this is the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*).
The position [is as follows]: || 10 || And one should consume [the portion] after the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*. || 31 ||

Regarding this, one might raise the objection that since there is a mention of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*)—namely, "the first draught belongs to the one who utters *vaṣaṭ*"—this is not an injunction for the act of drinking itself; however, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that it is indeed an injunction of a qualified action (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*). But surely, there is no qualified injunction here, for "firstness" is not a property of the act of drinking.
An agent by which an action qualified by a sacrifice might be enjoined.
For this very reason, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) raised the doubt that a qualified injunction is not possible here.

How, then, is the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*)? Because the two words "first" (*prathama*) and "consumption" (*bhakṣa*) express a single meaning, and because of the prescription of what has already been mentioned, one considers them to have a single referent. That is incorrect;
for even in a compound, there is no disappearance [of the individual meanings] according to the principle of the locus of that which has become so (*tadbhūtādhikaraṇanyāya*). This being true—
Even so, since in a compound the connection between word-meanings depends on the relationship between preceding and following words,
it is rightly said that for one who prescribes a compound, it is not difficult to enjoin multiple qualities.
Therefore, it is established that this is a qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhāna).
And [it is so] because of the two acts of pressing and offering. || 11 || || 32 ||
"Having pressed and having offered, he consumes"—this is also an injunction for consumption, because the acts of offering and pressing have already been established.
And because it is impossible for it to be prescribed as an auxiliary (aṅga), the act of eating itself must be what is prescribed.
|| 12 || Furthermore, because the cups (camasa) are directly taught [as primary], the remainder is indistinct [in its application]. || 33 ||

Based on scriptural passages such as "the Hotṛ’s cup" and other such designations, which indicate a connection with all the cups, one might think that the consumption [of the Soma] occurs elsewhere than in the cups, following the sequence "having pressed and having offered. This being the prima facie view, it is stated in reply: the consumption in the cups is caused by the acts of pressing and offering.
It is indeed so. But has it not been stated that the term "hotṛcamasa" conveys the understanding of the entire cup?

True, it has been so stated; however, it cannot negate its status as being caused by the pressing [of Soma]. These statements are merely indicative; once the relationship expressed by "hotṛcamasa" is understood, there is no exclusion of other relationships.

It can be understood because there is a comprehension of mere attainment (*prāpti*). For when attainment exists and there is the intention to express "to whom does this belong?", the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) is perceived. Just as, for example, when it is said "belonging to Agni" (*āgneya*), [the exclusion of others is understood].

In the case of the offering to Indra and Agni, there is no such comprehension [of exclusion]. Here, however, because the sentence has the attainment [of the cup] as its result, the exclusion of others cannot be understood. But surely, even in the case of attainment, a contradiction exists because of the comprehension of the whole [set of cups].
True; that would be so if the attainment were by means of the name (samākhyā). Here, however, it is by the text: "Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forward."
Because of the scriptural statement; and this must be inferred from the passage "having pressed [the juice] and having offered [it].
|| 13 || In a single vessel, the Adhvaryu priest should drink first in due order. || 36 ||
"The pressers and the Hotṛ priests consume [the Soma] from the cup that has been set down.
Now, it is considered here: who should consume first? The Adhvaryu consumes it because it is in his hand, according to the principle: "He whose hand holds it, he wins."
[Page b870] But surely it is said, "The first draught belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer. On account of this scriptural statement, how can there be a draught for the *adhvaryu*?
This is the thought of one who considers that even from the injunction regarding the mere act of drinking, the first draught belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer alone.
Furthermore, this is the subject under discussion. And it has been demonstrated that the *vaṣaṭ*-call comes first; thus, it was concluded with the words "and because of the scriptural statement.
|| 14 || "The consumption [of the soma] is permitted by virtue of the scriptural statement. || 40 ||

This section is intended to demonstrate the point of application: whether one should eat only what has been authorized or even what has not been authorized. In the absence of a specific statement, there is no restriction; however, due to the existence of a statement, there is a restriction.

[It is] thus. This restriction being established, is the request for permission to be made with a worldly word or with a Vedic one? Since no mantra is prescribed [for this], the restriction is that it must be done with a Vedic word. This [statement] also serves solely to demonstrate the application of the mantra.
15. In that case, the answer follows from the sense. 42.

Now, there is a doubt regarding the response: is the response to be made with a mantra or with ordinary speech? How, then, does the doubt arise from the recitation of the mantra "upahūta" (you are invited)? It arises for one who considers it to be the remainder of the very [mantra] "upahvayasva" (invite me). For [the mantra] was not recited prior to the request for permission.
The intention is that even though one is capable of providing a reply, one is nonetheless fit for giving a reply; however,
the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) has established his conclusion by asserting that in this case, the previous position alone is sublated.
16. [The rule applies] because of the assembly of those who share a single vessel. 43.
Regarding the recitation, the request for instruction, and the response, is the request for instruction intended only for those who share a single vessel, or is it without distinction?

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers it to be without distinction because there is no specific injunction to the contrary. However, the final established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that it is restricted by its visible purpose.
17. By the removal of the *yājyā*, the *bhakṣa* (consuming) is also removed, just like the *pravara*. 44.

The intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin), who considers that there is merely the removal of the *yājyā*, is that the consumption (*bhakṣa*) belongs to the Hotṛ alone. Does he not perceive the scriptural statement regarding the absence of breath-pause (*anavāna*), just as [one perceives] the statement "having sat down, he sacrifices"? No, he does not fail to perceive it; rather, he perceives it as applying to the *yājyā* alone. In this way, both of these [scriptural statements] are rendered consistent.

This is the intended meaning: the sense is that the agency of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is established by means of the designation of the *yājyā* verse. However, the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*) considers this: while it is indeed logically consistent, yet upon the removal of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, nothing [of the original status] remains.

Since there is authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) that the application of the *yājyā* formula is appropriate even when accompanied by the *svaṣaṭkāra*, it is logical that agency (*kartṛtva*) is established by accepting the performance of the action. As for the point that the *pravara* (the invocation of ancestral lineage) is not omitted,
it has already been demonstrated how the *pravara* is not omitted because it is based on direct scriptural injunction (*aupadeśika*).
The fruit-cup is a contingent modification of the consumption [of Soma], because of its connection with the Vedic text.
Is the fruit-cup a modification of the act of consumption (*bhakṣa*), or is it a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyā*)?

Regarding this doubt, we say: there is no doubt here at all, because [the text states], "One should offer that portion for him to consume" (*tamasmai bhakṣaṃ prayacchet*); thus, it is connected with consumption.

Because [the Soma] is enjoined as an accessory to the act of consuming (*bhakṣa*), it modifies the consumption, not the sacrifice. Nor can it be said that it modifies the sacrifice, because the Soma is prescribed by the original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*).
If it were enjoined [as an accessory to the sacrifice], there would be the contingency of a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*). Consequently, even the modification of the consumption would not occur.

The modification of the sacrifice is remote. To this it is replied: the fruit-cup (phalacamasa) is not capable of being modified without a modification of the sacrifice; for the consumption of Soma consists of the remnants of the sacrifice. And when that which is not a remnant is consumed, the sacrifice does not thereby become modified. Therefore, the status of being a sacrificial remnant belongs to the fruit—

The *camasa* cup must also be considered. Now, it was argued that because *soma* is prescribed as a primary element by its originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), its prescription in the sacrifice is not possible; for if it were prescribed by way of a reference to the sacrifice (*yāgānuvādena*), there would be a lack of recognition (*apratyabhijñāna*).
It is liberated; it is not, however, connected even with the effect (*kārya*). This connection exists precisely through the effect.

But surely, the Commentator, having raised the objection regarding the absence of a connection with the sacrifice, stated the connection as "one should cause to sacrifice" (*yājayet*), [using] the root *yaj*. That was said for the purpose of demonstrating the connection with the sacrifice.

Furthermore, there is no fault, as this is not for the purpose of restating what has already been enjoined. And the concluding statement, "one should perform the eating," clarifies this very point. Therefore, it is established that the *phalacamas* is a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyāvikāra*).
Moreover, the injunctions regarding its qualities have been demonstrated.

On one side, it is because the ritual items (*padārtha*) are prescribed [in that section]; on the other, it is because of their proximity (*samabhyāśīkaraṇa*). In that regard, by virtue of the specific designation (*viśeṣasamākhyā*), they belong to the sacrificer. As for the ritual items—
Because proximity is preceded by that [performance]. To this it is replied: the ritual acts (padārtha) belong exclusively to the Adhvaryu;
for as long as the act is not being performed, it is impossible for the sacrificer (yajamāna) to establish proximity with it.
It belongs to the Adhvaryu alone; for the application of specific designations has already been demonstrated.
[In case of] conflict, the instrumental [designation prevails] due to a specific connection; the other [designation applies] to those from which a specific distinction arises.

When there is an instruction regarding the duties of another officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a doubt arises as to whether he should perform his own specific task or that which is extended to him by analogy (*atidiṣṭa*). It is established that it is the extended duty, because of the direct injunction. || 11 || [In the case of] commands (*praiṣa*), [the rule applies] because they pertain to the authority of another. || 23 ||
Should the *praiṣa* (the command) and the purpose of the *praiṣa* be performed by one person, or by two?

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they should be performed by one, due to the misconception that the time has arrived. This involves the abandonment of the referent of the second-person pronoun (*yuṣmad-artha*).
The established conclusion is that it is due to the absence of a cause. And the Adhvaryu [is the one who performs it], because it is so seen.

Now, there arises the doubt: should the Adhvaryu perform the purpose of the *praiṣa* (direction), or someone else? It is initially argued that it should be someone else, because of the observation of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). However, [the conclusion is] that the Adhvaryu performs it, because of the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra, and because the meaning is possible through the name (*samākhyāna*). As for the explanatory passage, it is resolved by being understood as a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*).
The fruit belongs to the officiating priests because they are the instruments, as in the case of a sacrifice. 25.

What, then, is the distinction of this [rite] from the benedictory mantras? Since the agency of the Adhvaryu is established by the traditional designation (*samākhyā*), the injunction of the mantras for the *agnyanvādhāna* is based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Nor can it be argued that the primary agency should be sublated in deference to a subordinate factor (*guṇa*). Therefore, the mantras belong to the Adhvaryu.
This being established, it is considered whose benediction [is to be recited]. Based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it belongs to the Adhvaryu;

for the speaker is connected with the first person. But is it not the case that the mantras serve the purpose of the ritual because they proclaim a fruit connected to the ritual? No; since they manifest the glory (*yaśas*) occasioned by the ritual, their being for the purpose of the ritual is indeed appropriate.

Thus the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) thinks. But the proponent of the final conclusion (rāddhāntavādī), considering that "that which is a purpose by implication is not the purpose of the injunction," maintains that the mantra reveals only a fruit connected with the ritual action.

The fruit belongs to the ritual action; the result is connected exclusively to the sacrificer. The meaning of the mantra is "of me, the sacrificer. || 14 || But the fruit is for the sake of the ritual action, because it is purposeful with respect to its master (the sacrificer). || 28 ||

Furthermore, regarding that which has a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārtha), does it belong only to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), or is the fruit of the action (karmaphala) here also [the same]? According to the stated reasoning, we say that it is indeed the fruit of the action. To this it is replied:

"And that which is a benefit derived from another benefit is not the purpose of the injunction (codanārtha). This was said with the understanding that there is no assistance [to the primary act]. As for what...
Furthermore, it assists karma by virtue of being a remainder of its appropriation; since it indeed exists for the sake of karma,
mantras do not lack the purpose of karma.
And because of the designation [of the self]. || 29 ||
And where it is indeed specifically designated, there the observation of the result certainly occurs—thus, "that is for both of us.
|| 16 || The preparation of the substance [is determined] by the specific context. || 30 ||
It has been stated that "the altar and the properties of the altar" [are mentioned] with the intention of what is to be said later.
However, because of the specific designation, there is no application of the modified (vikṛta) apūrva.

In the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*), it is established that the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is for the sake of both the subsidiary and the principal acts. Now, regarding the modified rite (*vikṛti*), this is considered: do the ritual properties (*dharma*) apply to the grass here as well for the sake of both the subsidiary and the principal through the extended application (*codaka*), or are they applied only by virtue of the specific function of the archetypal grass? In this regard, as in the archetype, so in the modification—
The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that they are enjoined;

however, the proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*) [considers them] generally, by way of their function, as being connected to the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the principal rite.

The principle "as in the archetype, so in the ectype" refers to the determination of ritual properties (*dharma*) in the ectype; it does not mean that they apply simply because they were connected to the archetype. For if it were by virtue of a general connection, the instruction would apply everywhere, and consequently, the observation of *ūha* (modification) would be untenable. Therefore, it is established that [the rule] does not apply to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
The ritual properties of clarified butter (*ājya*) do not apply to collyrium (*añjana*).
|| 18 || And in case of conflict, because of the specific scriptural statement, the unmanifest [rule] applies to the remainder. || 32 ||
Since it is not logical for the status of being a remnant to apply in multiple locations, something other than the *paribhojanīya* (food for consumption) must be prepared.
But the two solstices [are determined] from a single location. || 33 ||

The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that, according to the principle of the preceding section, it is not logical for something to serve as a subsidiary (śeṣa-bhāva) to multiple things; this is the thought of the opponent. The established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that because of the restriction to two portions (dvayavadāna) and because it is a disposal (pratipatti), [the offering] is for all purposes in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti). || 20 || 2. The subsidiary is for the sake of all [purposes] in the modified sacrifice. || 34 ||
Now, the properties such as being performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) are considered.

The doubt is: do these properties there also serve both the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the primary (*pradhāna*) rites, just as in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), or not? The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the properties serve both the subsidiary and the primary rites, just as in the model sacrifice.

[Page b950] It is not the case that the extended application (*atideśa*) is connected with the direct instruction (*upadeśa*), because the extended application depends upon the direct instruction; this dependence is the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*). What, then, is the reason for this?

Is it connected? Since extension (*atideśa*) depends upon instruction (*upadeśa*), those who know the principles [of Mīmāṃsā] hold that between the dependent and the independent, the independent is stronger. || 21 || 1. When [the primary rite] is impossible due to a specific proximity, [the rule applies] to its subsidiaries. || 36 ||
In the case of the Śyena sacrifice, however, because there is an absence of an original (aupadeśika) connection, the connection is established solely through extension (ātideśika);
this is the distinction.
At that time, [it occurs] for you through the sight of the linga. || 39 ||

Now, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that, due to the appearance of an indicative mark (liṅga), the injunction here applies only to those [offerings] whose time is the Soma-pressing (sutyā). The established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that it applies to all of them, because there is no distinction.
|| 23 || But the meat belongs to the Savanīya offerings. || 42 ||

"The sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) for the Soma-pressings (savanīya) are [to be made] quickly. Here, since the simultaneous expression of both "Soma-pressing" and "sacrificial cake" would result in a syntactical split (vākya-bheda), the question arises as to which term is figurative.
It has been established as the final conclusion (rāddhāntita) that the term "sacrificial cake" is figurative, because its deviation from the literal sense is observed.
Thus ends the eighth quarter of the third chapter in the Bṛhatī.
The first quarter of the fourth chapter.
1. Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into that which is for the sake of the sacrifice and that which is for the sake of the person.
Why is the inquiry into that which subserves the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and that which subserves the person (*puruṣārtha*) proposed separately?

For subserviency (*śeṣatva*) is indeed characterized by being for the sake of this (*aidamarthya*), as it has been stated: "The subordinate is so because it exists for the sake of another. Furthermore, subservience to the sacrifice is also included within that [general definition] and was already proposed by the statement: "Now, therefore, the definition of the subordinate."
Therefore, we do not see the purpose of restating the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Now, if it is thought that the status of being a human goal (*puruṣārthatā*) is not understood through direct audition (*śruti*) and so forth, because of the desire for its acquisition—

He will state [later] that it is a definition (*lakṣaṇā*). In that case, the mention of "being for the sake of the sacrifice" (*kratvartha*) has been refuted. Nor can this also be called a definition of "being for the sake of the person" (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, the cognition that "the sacrifice is for the sake of heaven" does not arise from the word itself; nor does the cognition that "heaven, which is to be accomplished by that [sacrifice], is for the sake of the person" arise inherently.

Furthermore, the mention of "samādhi" is also redundant. We do not understand for what purpose even that mention of "direct assertion" (*śruti*) and the rest is made; for the definition of the subordinate (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be established by any means other than direct assertion and so forth. Therefore, it would have been sufficient simply to say "the definition of the subordinate. Consequently, the mention of "direct assertion" and the rest serves no significant purpose.

It appears as if [the author] were addressing a common person. Furthermore, his recounting of the propositions while including within them the categories of the "prompter" (*prayojaka*) and "non-prompter" (*aprayojaka*) regarding what serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) is also, as it were, inconsistent.
Why? Because inclusion occurs either by way of essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), by way of definition (*lakṣaṇataḥ*), or by way of function (*kāryataḥ*).
All three of these are absent here. First, the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is distinct simply because it is designated separately.
The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is also distinct precisely because of the difference in intrinsic nature. Apart from a difference in characteristics, there is no difference in intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, that which was shown by the author of the Bhāṣya regarding the "thing to be accomplished" (kārya) is incorrect; for an explanatory passage (arthavāda) that contradicts other sections serves the purpose of praise, and even primacy is based upon the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor.
Even that which is the motivator (prayojaka) establishes its own primacy with respect to the motivated (prayojya). It is not...
Furthermore, regarding his own altruism: this commentary, like setting out on a journey at night without a guide,
produces confusion.
To this it is replied: both of these—the presentation of distinction and the inclusion—are appropriate, just as in that [previous] case.

As for the statement that "the fact of being for the sake of that (tādarthya) is the reason for subsidiarity (śeṣatva), provided that direct assertion (śruti) and the other criteria exist," [it means that] although it has been stated that the subservience to the ritual (kratvarthatā) is thereby refuted, [this objection is not valid].

This would be so if it were said to be based on *viniyoga* (application). But here, he asserts that it is based solely on *upādāna* (appropriation). What is meant by "appropriation"? Appropriation is the implication (*ākṣepa*) of an injunction (*niyoga*).

And it is due to that [appropriation] that the sprinkling and other such acts have their purpose in the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*). On the other hand, through *viniyoga*, they would have their purpose in the rice-grains (*vrīhyarthatā*) alone.
[Page b957] Then what is the claim regarding their distinction? And why is there inclusion?
Distinction arises from the difference in the causes of comprehension; inclusion arises from the commonality of the assistance rendered. There is some motivating factor [for this].

The mention of "human purpose" (*puruṣārtha*) is for the purpose of making known that even something which is a motivator may not be a human purpose—for example, the recitation of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) in relation to the injunction to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*).
[This is because] there is a desire for that in which a person finds pleasure, since the desire for it is not distinct from the definition of a human purpose. (JS 4.1.2)
"It arises solely through the desire for acquisition, not through the treatise"—
this has been stated contradictorily.
Heaven is not understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) apart from the scripture, nor is it understood as residing in the agent.

This was stated with reference to the scripture of relationship (*saṃbandha-śāstra*). Furthermore, the purpose (*artha*) is the fulfillment of the injunction (*niyoga*), and that is what constitutes "appropriation" (*upādāna*), as has been said. But is it not the case that being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*) is also stated by means of appropriation? [This is so] in the context of application (*viniyoga*).
It has been stated that "it exists. For it is precisely from the meaning itself that the distinction arises, namely, that it is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
What is meant by this phrase "due to non-distinction" (*avibhāgāt*)? It means due to the non-distinction of the person's connection with the ritual (*kratu*).

And we shall establish this more precisely in the sixth [book]. Since the application [of the elements] occurs by way of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*), it follows that they serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Or rather: [one might object], "But was it not already stated that these are injunctions regarding qualities and results (*guṇaphalacodanā*)? What then is this..."
What is the further deliberation? It is said: we have already shown that it was stated on the basis of application (*viniyoga*).
Here, however, since a visible purpose is possible based on the material cause (*upādāna*), an invisible purpose is not possible;
such is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

No, because the function is understood according to the specific application (*viniyoga*). For the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that the postulation of a function applies only to that which has been specifically enjoined, and not to that which has not been so enjoined.

Therefore, it is established that, by virtue of application (*viniyoga*) and material cause (*upādāna*), the injunctions regarding the fruits of the qualities (*guṇaphala-codanā*) have as their sole purpose the aim of man (*puruṣārtha*). The mention of Bādari, moreover, is for the sake of demonstrating the benefit; it is not, however, for the sake of negating the reason of being a "subsidiary" (*śeṣa*) on the grounds of being for the sake of another (*parārthatva*). How so? For in the case of application...

It has been stated: "But surely Bādari also proposed this very application; for that very reason it was rejected. Here, however, it is proposed that the inclusion is based precisely on the function (*kārya*).

There is no contradiction in the fact that [the injunction] is set aside due to improper application. Or rather, as follows: here, the rules regarding the acquisition of property serve as the examples. In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: because the injunctions of restrictive rules (*niyama-niyoga*) lack a specific qualification (*adhikāra*), they form a single syntactical unit with the injunctions of desire (*kāma-śruti*). Therefore—

Because [the ownership] is established by the act [of giving]. And in this way, it is clearly established that even the *kṣāmavatī* offerings and others serve the purpose of the ritual (*karmārthatā*).
Therefore, so that the injunction does not become meaningless for one who lacks the qualification [to own property], it must serve the purpose of the ritual.
[Objection: But if it serves the purpose of the ritual, then there would be no ownership at all, and thus the sacrifice itself could not be accomplished.
This was merely a frivolous statement by someone:
that acquisition does not produce ownership is a contradiction. How then [is it so]?
[Objection: Is it for the sake of the sacrifice? The intention is that ownership exists for that purpose, just as in the case of the *vanīvāhana* (the repeated driving of the chariot).
To this, it is replied: These restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*) cannot be said to be devoid of a qualified person (*adhikāra*).
Those who have engaged in [the activity] for the sake of livelihood will be the qualified persons.

Nor is entitlement derived from the word alone; rather, it is from entitlement itself that there is entitlement. That [entitlement], however, is sometimes understood through the word and sometimes understood through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, regarding ownership—
Because all human goals are accomplished through specific [means], no further distinction can be determined.

Moreover, if the substance intended for ritual action according to the scripture were not to be employed elsewhere, then that which has been acquired would result in the total collapse of the entire system. What is the meaning? What is this?

If it is argued that "tantra" means "life," then life will continue because there is no fixed rule; for a fixed rule exists only for the sake of the ritual (*kratu*). Alternatively, if it is intended that other rituals are what is denoted by the word "tantra," even so, there is no omission, because there is a fixed rule for each individual ritual.
To this it is replied: what is intended by the term *tantra* here are indeed other sacrifices (*kratvantara*).
Furthermore, there is no evidence for the claim that acquisition (*arjana*) involves the adoption of specific details. Nor is every *tantra* performed by everyone.
If it were possible to perform [the rite] by means of a single substance, there would be an omission of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for all the constituent acts;

furthermore, this is another fault: the view that one ritual procedure is not extended while another ritual procedure is being extended is untenable. If, on the other hand, this [substance] is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to any single [act], then in that case, this [view] is simply not [correct].
It is grasped by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*); for that which is not grasped by the injunction of performance lacks the very status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*).

Since there is no status as an auxiliary, it is said that for whatever lacks the status of an auxiliary, there is a lack of assistance through performance; thus, this very absence of auxiliary status is shown by way of non-assistance.
Nor can it be like the act of kindling (ādhāna). This sweeping (mārjana) cannot be for the sake of the substance alone,
nor can it be for the sake of the fire alone like the kindling, because it is understood that the qualification for the rite belongs to one who is engaged in living.

Therefore, this cleansing (*ārjana*) is for the sake of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) alone. Consequently, if it were for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), the established defect would be the omission of the *tantra* (the common ritual procedure). Since the *kṣāmavati* offerings and others are understood to pertain to one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), let them be for the sake of the sacrifice, with their fruit to be inferred; or rather, let them be occasional rites (*naimittika*) for the human goal alone.

Therefore, it is established that the rules for acquiring property are for the sake of the human agent; hence, the transgression of these rules results in harm to the person, not to the sacrifice. For when such [rules] are set aside, the scripture remains beyond doubt regarding its purpose for the benefit of the person in the performance of ritual action.
And a substance is not intended to be brought about; therefore, because of its connection with that purpose, the mention of the person [is made] in relation to the action. || 3 ||

It has been stated that whatever brings pleasure to a person, there is a desire for it, which is the characteristic of an object of pursuit (*artha*). However, in this case, since pleasure is not explicitly heard and its implication is not understood from the context, the qualification (*adhikārin*)— [p. b966] ...is not established. Thus, because of the absence of a specific injunction (*vidhi*), the *arthavāda* passages are merely intended to praise the *agnihotra*. Furthermore, since there is no other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish the connection between the *agnihotra* and heaven, the *arthavāda* cannot serve as a basis for such a connection. Moreover, the word "heaven" (*svarga*) is used here in the sense of happiness (*sukha*), and happiness is not established by the mere performance of the *agnihotra*. Therefore, the *arthavāda* does not possess the capacity to convey the relationship between the *agnihotra* and heaven. Consequently, the *agnihotra* must be understood as having heaven as its fruit through the force of an injunction (*codanā*). And since the injunction is established by the *arthavāda*, the *arthavāda* is indeed a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge for the purpose of praising the *agnihotra*. (JS 1.2.7) Furthermore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge because it possesses the capacity to convey meaning. For example, when one hears the statement, "The *udumbara* tree is full of vigor," a desire arises to obtain an *udumbara* branch. This is because the statement is connected with a result; otherwise, it would be meaningless. Since the *udumbara* branch is not something already established by another means of knowledge, the statement is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Nor can it be considered a false assertion, for it is not contradicted by perception or other means of knowledge. Therefore, the statement "The *udumbara* tree is full of vigor" is a means of valid knowledge. Similarly, the *arthavāda* statements, "He who knows thus, he who performs thus," and so forth, are means of valid knowledge. Furthermore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge because it is connected with the *codanā* (injunction). For instance, in the passage, "One should offer the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices for the attainment of heaven; he who, knowing thus, performs the new and full moon sacrifices, becomes possessed of cattle," the *arthavāda*—"He becomes possessed of cattle"—is connected with the injunction. If it were not so, the injunction would lack a fruit and would be meaningless. Therefore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge. (JS 1.2.8) Moreover, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge because it is connected with the *mantra*. For example, in the passage, "He who knows thus, he who performs thus, cuts the sacrificial post of *parṇa* wood; he who cuts the *parṇa* post attains immortality," the *arthavāda*—"He attains immortality"—is connected with the *mantra* "He cuts the *parṇa* post. If it were not so, the *mantra* would be meaningless. Therefore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge. (JS 1.2.9) Furthermore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge because it is connected with the name (*nāmadheya*). For example, in the passage, "He who knows thus, he who performs thus, offers the *vaiśvānara* oblation; he who offers the *vaiśvānara* oblation conquers these worlds," the *arthavāda*—"He conquers these worlds"—is connected with the name "vaiśvānara. If it were not so, the name would be meaningless. Therefore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge. (JS 1.2.10) Finally, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge because it is connected with the *dharma*. For example, in the passage, "He who knows thus, he who performs thus, offers the *agnihotra*; he who offers the *agnihotra* reaches the world of heaven," the *arthavāda*—"He reaches the world of heaven"—is connected with the *dharma* of the *agnihotra*. If it were not so, the *dharma* would be meaningless. Therefore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge. (JS 1.2.11) Thus, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge because it possesses the capacity to convey meaning, is connected with the injunction, the *mantra*, the name, and the *dharma*. (JS 1.2.12) Furthermore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge because it is connected with the *upamāna* (analogy). For example, in the passage, "As is the *yajñāyajñīya* chant, so is the *gāyatrī* meter," the *arthavāda* is connected with the analogy. If it were not so, the analogy would be meaningless. Therefore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge. (JS 1.2.13) In this way, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge because it possesses the capacity to convey meaning and is connected with the injunction, the *mantra*, the name, the *dharma*, and the analogy. (JS 1.2.14) Furthermore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge because it is connected with the *itihāsa* (ancient lore) and *purāṇa* (legend). For example, in the passage, "The gods and the Asuras contended; the gods won by means of the *bhūḥ* exclamation," the *arthavāda* is connected with the *itihāsa* and *purāṇa*. If it were not so, the *itihāsa* and *purāṇa* would be meaningless. Therefore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge. (JS 1.2.15) Thus, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge because it possesses the capacity to convey meaning and is connected with the injunction, the *mantra*, the name, the *dharma*, the analogy, the *itihāsa*, and the *purāṇa*. (JS 1.2.16) Furthermore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge because it is connected with the *liṅga* (indicative mark). For example, in the passage, "The *barhis* grass is the earth; the *ājya* is Agni; the *puroḍāśa* is Soma," the *arthavāda* is connected with the indicative mark. If it were not so, the indicative mark would be meaningless. Therefore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge. (JS 1.2.17) Thus, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge because it possesses the capacity to convey meaning and is connected with the injunction, the *mantra*, the name, the *dharma*, the analogy, the *itihāsa*, the *purāṇa*, and the indicative mark. Therefore, the *arthavāda* is a means of valid knowledge.
