This is because the injunction [prescribes] emptiness, and that which lacks a qualification cannot constitute a human goal; therefore, this prohibition or restriction applies specifically to that looking which serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). To this, it is replied: this has already been stated regarding the relinquishment of pleasure (*prītyutsarga*); even though no qualification is explicitly heard, it is proper to assume a qualification.
Nor, however, is there the assumption of a connection with a ritual (*kratu*). What, then, is the distinction here?
This is the distinction: just as when a qualification (*adhikāra*) is heard, it is logical that its implied agent (*kartṛ*) alone [is understood].

Thus, since the agent who is currently engaged in the action (*gamyamāna*) is understood, it is only logical to assume a qualification (*adhikāra*). How then is there a "section on the agent" (*kartradhikaraṇa*)? For in that case, the application (*viniyoga*) serves as an opponent to the assumption of a qualification; here, however, the assumption of a qualification is without such an opponent. What kind [of agent] is it?
Furthermore, who is qualified for this? Since it is heard in scripture that "by this much one becomes freed from sin," the qualification belongs to one who is still living.

Therefore, this eternal rule (niyama) must be observed throughout one’s life as one’s own duty (svadharma). But is it not the case that a simple negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha) would be more logical? True; however, because of the understanding of the syntactical connection (anvaya) with the word "vow" (vrata), it is understood as an affirming negation (paryudāsa).

It is indeed logical that it has only a characteristic (lakṣaṇa) purpose. Furthermore, as in the case of the fire-consecration (ādhāna), a material purpose is not possible here either, because there is no connection with an unassigned substance and because no visible refinement (saṃskāra) exists.
Can it be said that it has a visible purpose? Certainly it can, like the wiping of a mirror.

Because their utility is observed in the world itself, it is therefore logical that the purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*) is the restrictive rule (*niyama*). Furthermore, since a visible purpose is impossible [in this case], it has been stated that even the *karkarī* (a type of water-vessel) and the *karṇa* (ear-ornament) serve the purpose of man.
But substances, because they are not specifically distinguished [in the injunction], should be offered, lest they be rendered purposeless. || 7 ||
It has been stated regarding these two [passages]: "The wooden sword and the potsherds," and "He digs with the wooden sword."

What is the factor that determines the application [of a word]? Regarding this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers "sphya, etc., are sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhāni*) to be a separate injunction, because through sentences such as "he digs with the *sphya*," a direct connection to the sacrifice is not perceived. But is it not the case that [the term "sacrificial implement"] is like [the expression] "the sacrificial post of the *vājapeya*"?
A connection is possible even by way of mediation. It is appropriate that, due to the absence of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), there is none in that case;
but here, what is not possible? This is the intended meaning. When this position has been reached, it is said: regarding the sacrifice—
In that case, there would be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the term *yudhāni*. If there is figurative indication, there is no difference between direct denotation and mediation;

for figurative indication follows another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And when a [direct] means of knowledge is already present, it is not possible to postulate another means of knowledge. This applies to both cases, such as "he digs with a wooden sword" (*sphya*);...
Because it is established; and thus the fault of conceptual construction is avoided, and the logical mark (*liṅga*) also becomes valid.
And in that case, singleness is not a constituent part of the sacrifice, because the object [of the action] is subordinate. || 11 ||

The opponent’s position is that oneness is not a constituent part of the sacrifice because it lacks a specific application (*viniyoga*). But how is it that oneness is not applied? For case-endings (*vibhakti*) express the connection of the nominal stem’s meaning with their own respective meanings. Therefore, both oneness and instrumentality [are expressed].

It belongs to the meaning of the nominal stem itself; it is not the singularity that possesses the status of being the instrument. For if there were a connection with the instrument, there could be no connection with the meaning of the nominal stem. As in the case of [the word] "arūṇayā" (with the red one), it is not so.

Therefore, even though this [quality] is perceived through a substance, it is not connected with the action, just as in the case of "the eastern one runs," which gives rise to the cognition of the "other" (western). And thus, the observations of indicative marks (*liṅga*) become consistent.
This being the position reached, it is said: It is not from the application (*viniyoga*) alone that there is subsidiariness to the action; what then?

For remainder also arises from the act of taking up (*upādāna*). Just as there is a taking up of that which has become an instrument (*karaṇa*), so too there is a taking up of that which is associated with oneness. For there is no taking up of that which is not an agent (*akāraka*), nor of that which lacks number.

It is possible even for one who is reasoning correctly; and thus worldly people understand in exactly that way when [instructed] with "Bring the cow" and so forth. This is what was stated: "The scripture does not say that the sentence-meaning does not exist [once it has been cognized]."

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that *viniyoga* (application) does not state that there is no *upādāna* (material cause). Now, one might object: "Does *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) not state that the meaning of the sentence does not exist?"
A different meaning indeed is understood. What meaning? This meaning is understood:

there is no contradiction of the sentence-meaning by the direct statement (*śruti*). Without abandoning the meaning of the direct statement, the fact that [the act] is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*) is understood from the sentence. It has been stated that in the case of a contradiction, there is weakness [of the sentence].

We have already stated that application (*viniyoga*) is not possible in the case of the singularity of the instrument (*karaṇa*). How, then, is the word "sentence" (*vākya*) used? This is a synonym for "collocation" (*samabhivyāhāra*), not for "application."
This is a synonym for *jak*. Therefore, it is established that number and gender are subordinate by virtue of being dependent [on the noun].
Thus, the various views are justified, and the view of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is a restatement.
Or rather: the section concerning gender (*liṅgādhikaraṇa*) is again "or rather" (*evaṃ vā*).

What is the intention of one who speaks thus? The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that the indicative mark (liṅga) is non-determinative; for number, as a determiner, expresses the dimension (parimāṇa) of a substance.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that because there is no distinction in the scriptural statement (*śravaṇa*), the indicative mark (*liṅga*) should also be adopted. Now, it was argued that the indicative mark should not be adopted because it results in a lack of definite measure (*apari-māṇa*). However, measure is not required for adoption here, because adoption is directed toward a specific [textual] particularity (*viśeṣa*), just as in the case of ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*).
Likewise, there is an expectancy for a specific [quality], as well as an expectancy for a specific agent. Therefore, it is established that it is mentioned just like number. The rest is as before.
|| 7 || 1. In the case of dependent [actions], the meaning of the verbal root would be understood without distinction. || 18 ||
In this context, the categories that reside [in a substratum] serve as the examples. Now, is the Bhāṣya incorrect?

Is it merely the sacrifice that is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the deity, or is an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) produced in the deity by means of the sacrifice? For if it were merely a refinement, it would be purposeless if it did not produce an unseen force.

It is stated that there are two kinds of injunctive statements (*ākhyāta*): those that enjoin what has not yet been attained, and those that restate an injunction already understood from another source. For example, the statement "he threshes" restates an injunction already apprehended through the primary injunctions such as the Āgneya sacrifice; it serves as the basis for qualification (*adhikāra*) by virtue of its connection with its own specific injunction.

And as for the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*): here now a doubt arises—whether it consists of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of an injunction (*niyoga*) already obtained by another, or whether it is a means of qualification (*adhikāra-sādhana*) through its connection with its own injunction? Why this doubt?
Because, according to the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), there is the possibility of what is seen in one part and what is unseen in another part; [and] regarding the seen...

He considers that it is not logical to assume an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) when a visible one is possible; thus, he regards [the opponent's position] as a mere restatement of what has been attained by another. [The opponent objects:

"But surely the meaning of 'sacrifice' (*yaj*) is not accomplished here. Its purpose will be the attainment of an unseen result through performance. To this, it is replied: its purpose is indeed only the attainment of a visible result.
This is not tenable. Why? Because the establishment of the mandate (*niyoga*) is not intended [as the primary goal].
For activity toward the object of the mandate proceeds from the mandate itself. Now, if there were a mandate for origination for that purpose...

The fact that [the injunction] has an unprecedented purpose (*apūrvārthatva*) is established as intended to be expressed. Subsequently, when the sacrifice is determined to have the purpose of the governing injunction (*adhikāraniyoga*), and once its connection with the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) has been defined, it is indeed accepted that [the injunction] functions through those subsidiaries for the sake of accomplishing visible purificatory effects (*dṛṣṭasaṃskāra*) pertaining to the substance and the deity. Nor is this a third mode [of operation] for the accomplishment of the governing injunction.

Because it is equal [to other rites], like the *samit* and so forth; whether the purpose be visible (*dṛṣṭa*) or invisible (*adṛṣṭa*), and whether the performance or non-performance be dictated by that purpose, in every respect its status as having its own specific injunction (*svaniyoga*) is established.
[Page b977] || 8 || Therefore, there is equality or inequality in the objects of the substances and their actions. || 21 ||
‘He has transcended the third stage.
What is this third stage? It is the cognition of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*). That has been transcended. Now, however, since being for the sake of another is established...
Only the appropriation itself is being considered: for what purpose is there appropriation, and for what purpose is there none?

But has not the consideration of appropriation already been made on the basis of purpose even prior to this? By what distinction is it said that "this [is discussed] now"? True—but its being for the sake of another is also caused by that [purpose].
It is for this very reason, and not because it is caused by a specific application (*viniyoga*), that it is said to be "within the scope of the third" (*tṛtīyaviṣaya*).

This is its scope as the third [subject], but it cannot be understood by means of the three instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, in the fourth [section], it is established that its subservience to another (*pārārthya*) is caused solely by an injunction (*vidhi*).

This was reflected upon, and it has already been explained—that it is not possible to establish the fact that everything exists for the sake of another through scripture and other means. This very point is stated here. And so:

Because of the qualification regarding the sacrifice and its fruit, [Bādarāyaṇa] will state that [the subordinate status] is for the sake of another. For this very reason, Bādarī held the misconception that subordination (śeṣatva) exists only in the case of substances, qualities, and purificatory acts (saṃskāra). This was because he saw the possibility of [subordination] through direct statement and so forth in those cases of substance and the rest, but failed to perceive the functional capacity of the "appropriation" (upādāna) and "qualification" (adhikāra).
Because of its retention. For this very reason, even though there is equality in the understanding of the remainder, another definition is stated:
"Because they are accomplished by a single [act], everything should be equal. (Sūtra 12)
From this point forward, only the operation of *upādāna* (presumption) is now considered;

however, the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣatā*) arises solely from *viniyoga* (application), not from *upādāna*. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), however, asserts *upādāna* based merely on the observation of a benefit (*upakāra*), and not [based on] its status as a subordinate.
[The opponent] thinks that it is to be expected, just as in the case of the "oneness of the animal" and so forth when there is a remainder of the material for the ritual (*upādānaśeṣa*).
Therefore, both [the purpose and the remainder] are motivators (*prayojaka*). To this, it is replied: here there is no status of being a motivator.
[This applies] to the *vājina* [offering]. Why? Because that which has become a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) possesses a requirement for a purpose (*prayojana*).

And since that requirement is satisfied by the very purpose belonging to that of which it is subordinate, it does not require another purpose as its motivator (*prayojaka*). How, then, can there be a state of being subordinate to the act of taking up (*upādāna-śeṣatva*) for that which is not subordinate [to anything else], such as singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth?

"There is no desire for a purpose whatsoever in that which is not a subordinate element (*aśeṣabhūta*), because if it were not subordinate, the very act of taking it up (*upādāna*) would be impossible. To this it is replied: because there is cognition of what is subordinate, and because there is no cognition otherwise, and because taking up is preceded by cognition; furthermore, because that which is subordinate is something to be employed (*prayojya*).
Because that would be untenable. For it has already been stated that what is unconditioned cannot be taken up.
Furthermore, that which is neither a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) nor perceived as residing within a subordinate element is not [taken up] by the taking up of the subordinate element.

That which is merely looked upon cannot be the motive for action; as it has been demonstrated in the Bhāṣya, just as the bringing of curd is not a subsidiary part of the whey, so too has the indicative mark (liṅga) been shown.
The ritual act of placing [the fire] is not the motive for the bringing [of the fire], because it serves another purpose. || 25 ||
What, then, is the distinction of this from the preceding case?

This is the distinction: for in that case, the bringing of the curds produces the whey (*vājina*) at the very same time as the production of the clotted curd (*āmikṣā*). Therefore, it is appropriate [to consider the whey] as a by-product.

There is a dependence on another cause. Here, however, when the "seventh step" is mentioned, an expectation arises as to whose [step it is]; because of the context, it is understood to be that of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*).
Therefore, one considers the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) to serve both purposes. This being the position reached, it is replied:

True, if an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to "whose [is it]? were possible; for when a related entity is taught whose other relation is not yet known, cognition arises preceded by such expectancy. But where there is no prior [expectancy for] another related entity...

Such is the instruction. In that regard, it has been shown in the case of the acceptance of a horse (*aśvapratigraha*) that the instruction must be preceded by a known relationship. Therefore, the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) intended for purchase is not employed as being connected to the seventh step.
On this point, the Bhāṣya says: "By one who relies upon the incidental application (*prasaṅga*)."
[Objection: But this is the definition of the *prayojana* (purpose).

What occasion is there for a *prasaṅga* (reductio)? For a *prasaṅga* is stated only when there exists a state of being a motivator (*prayojakatva*). However, in this case, there is no state of being a motivator at all. [Response: It is said: [this is] a *prasaṅga* within the context of the treatise (*śāstra*).
This was stated having provisionally accepted that point; there is no fault, as it does not entail the application [of the rule].
b982] || 11 || Furthermore, the action of denoting the meaning will occur because the connection has that [action] as its cause.
For that purpose indeed it is enjoined. || 26 ||

Regarding the statement, "He winnows the husks with the potsherd of the *puroḍāśa*," the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that there is no possibility of the scriptural injunction (*śāstra*) applying here, and thus [the potsherd] possesses the status of an instrument (*prayoktṛtva*).

Nor can it be said that the addition of the husks (*tuṣopavāpa*) is not invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*), as in the case of the whey (*vājina*). Therefore, both are motivators (*prayojaka*). To this, it is replied: True, there is no occasion for the application of scripture (*śāstra*) regarding the actual application (*viniyoga*); nor is it invariably concomitant.
[The opponent says:

It is a real entity (bhāva). However, since this is the application (*viniyoga*) of what has already been acquired, the postulation of an act of acquisition (*upādāna*) does not apply. This is what was stated: “This is a connection with that which is yet to be; it is not with that which is past or present.”
"By these two.

But if, on the other hand, there were a connection with the past and the present, what would be the basis [for the injunction]? It is said: not for the past, because that has already been taken up as having a future purpose.

The preservation of this very [thing] will occur, because the material cause (*upādāna*) is precisely that which constitutes preservation. Even for that which is currently existing, it is impossible to employ its constituent part elsewhere; thus, by implication, another thing must be taken up as the material cause. However, if the purpose pertains to the future, then there is the employment of what has been acquired for one purpose toward another.

It is established that [the reason] is not probative (*aprayojaka*) because [the conclusion] is possible [otherwise]. However, whether the scattering of husks (*tuṣopavāpa*) should be performed or not performed is not the subject matter of this section (*adhikaraṇa*).
12. Because there is no immolation of the sacrificial animal, blood and excrement do not constitute part of the ritual action. 27.

In this discussion, the injunction regarding the cutting out of the heart and other organs, as well as the injunction regarding the discharge of blood and excrement, are equal. The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers both to have the status of motivators (*prayojaka*) because they pertain to the animal sacrifice under discussion, namely, "One should immolate the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma."

To this it is replied: the statement "one should cut portions from the heart first" is a concluding reference to the sacrifice, because of the scriptural hearing that "the [sacrificial] limbs [are used] at the third pressing."
But that which is simultaneously established (*sakṛtsaṃpravyādha*) is so because it terminates at that very point and because it takes the subject under discussion as its basis.
Furthermore, comprehension (*pratipatti*) is not the motive; the object to be communicated is not employed for the sake of comprehension.
According to this principle, therefore, the dung and other parts of the animal are not the motivators [of the action].
|| 13 || And that which has a substance consisting of a single part [is not a motivator], because of its connection with what already exists at the time of origin. || 28 ||

But surely, even the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here is untenable; for the understanding of the "remnant" (*śeṣa*) arises from the fact that it refers to a substance already taken up, just as in the case of a piece of sugar-cane. True, this is so; however, since the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) here serves another purpose, its application to a different function elsewhere is not tenable.

Therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that another substance must be taken up. The proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntavādī*), however, holds that there is no requirement to bring in [another substance] beyond the mere two portions; for the *Āgneya* sacrifice is accomplished by the mere two portions alone.

He stated that the reabsorption (*saṃhāra*) is for the purpose of making its application elsewhere possible; for if it were given to another, then, being intended for the sake of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*), that [reabsorption] would not be tenable. Therefore, its application elsewhere than in the function of sacrifice (*yāga*) is impossible. Furthermore, because it serves the function of sacrifice, it cannot have any other purpose.
It can be stated that, therefore, there is no contradiction with the injunctions for the Āgneya and other offerings.

Consequently, it is established—according to the maxim of the unopposed piece of sugarcane—that [the whole] is not to be taken; as it was said in the Bhāṣya: "Because of the observation of the remnants, the scriptural statement regarding the *samavadāna* (equal portioning) is likewise [to be understood]."
14. In the case of the pouring over (abhighāraṇa), there should be a separation of vessels due to the distance [of the action], as in the case of the after-sacrifices (anuyāja).

[Page b987] But what, then, is distinguished here by the *puroḍāśa*-pan? It is already established that there is no taking up of a substance in that manner. However, the taking up of the oblation (*havis*) is for the purpose of supporting it.

The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that [the sprinkling] does not contradict [the purpose of the offering] because of the predominance [of the oblation], and not because it serves another purpose. But how is there predominance of the oblation? Because the accusative case-ending is heard [in the text], and because the sprinkling is for its sake;
and because the remnant of the Prayāja offerings is for its sake, just like the potsherds of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that it is not logical for the oblations to have primacy because the clarified butter (*ājya*) serves a visible purpose;
therefore, this is merely a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings. How then are the oblations—

The plural number [in "abhighārayati"] is used because the act of pouring over is accomplished with a single oblation; since no specific distinction is being grasped, the plural is not contradictory. Therefore, just like the taking up of the substance, the taking up for the purpose of holding is also not appropriate, because the disposal (*pratipatti*) is accomplished in the very oblation that is present.
Thus [it is said].

Now, one might object: it is not possible to understand the second and third [statements] as having a different meaning, because there is no contradiction with the literal sense of the words. True; this would be so if the statement were non-contradictory. But in this case, however—

This contradicts the term *prayājaśeṣa* (the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings); however, in the case of a disposal (*pratipatti*), there is no such contradiction. Therefore, it is logical that the case-ending, which expresses a subordinate sense, conforms to the meaning of the nominal stem.

In this case as well, it is logical that [the locative] has another meaning; for when two actions occur in a single sentence, the meaning of the locative should be understood as being consistent with their connection. The [meaning of] "seeing" has already been stated.
"But the bringing together (samānayana) should be primary, because of the observation of an indicative mark. (Sūtra 40)

Regarding the statement, “Having passed over the iḍā, he pours together [the butter] upon the sacrificial grass (barhis),” there is a doubt: is this pouring together intended solely for the sake of the two subsequent prayāja offerings?

And from that [it follows]: is this [the act of pouring] the instigator of the *aupabhṛta* clarified butter intended for the *prayāja*s and *anūyāja*s, as well as of their ritual properties (*dharma*s)?

Or rather, is this solely for the purpose of mixing, being for the sake of the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *jauhava* [butter]? And consequently, since it is to be accomplished by means of a substance employed for another purpose, the clarified butter and its ritual properties are not instigators. In that regard, the former—

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) understands the act of "bringing together" (samānayana) to be merely a mixing, based solely on the scriptural mention of it. Furthermore, he maintains that the injunction "one takes eight [spoonfuls] in the upabhṛt vessel" serves the purpose of all the prayāja offerings. Why?
Because no specific distinction is heard in the text. Therefore, this act of bringing together has only an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose.
This being the case, it is replied: this bringing together (*samānayana*) is for the sake of accomplishing the two *prayāja* offerings.
Why? Because in this way the bringing together serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*), as does the drawing [of butter] into the *upabhṛt* ladle for the sake of the *prayāja*s.

But surely, that which is contained in the *aupabhṛta* vessel is heard in scripture as being for all purposes without distinction; and it is logical that its purpose be unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), in accordance with what is heard in scripture. A scriptural statement of no distinction cannot be restricted to a specific case by means of functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).

Being thus established, it abandons the status of being the meaning of a word. Therefore, since the word is not obstructed, the view of the established conclusion (rāddhānta) has been stated: when a perceptible [explanation] is possible, the postulation of an imperceptible one is not logical.
In that case, the origin would be undivided. || 42 ||
What, then, is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) who asserts that "both [the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*] are for both purposes"? This is the intention:

because it is heard without distinction that "one takes four [ladlefuls] in the *juhū*," and because the accomplishment of the ritual task is achieved specifically through the taking for the *prayāja*s, [the taking] for the *anūyāja*s—
In the *Jauhaba*, it is considered a mere repetitive restatement (*anuvāda*) of what has already been said.
To this, it is replied: if the attainment were indeed obtained solely through the material cause (*upādāna*), then this would be so.

Because the dual purpose is understood from the mere mention of the *upabhṛt* vessel itself. If that is so, then let the *aupabhṛta* [clarified butter] be for the sake of the *anūyāja* offerings alone, since it is heard in scripture as being solely for the *anūyāja*. It is replied: because this injunctive statement already has its purpose established, it is considered a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that which is already connected with the *anūyāja* alone.
Whence is this acquisition? It is from the statement, "He takes it for the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s," because it serves both purposes.
But surely, since the point was already settled in the section concerning the *samānayana* (the pouring together), how can this doubt be raised now?
For in that [section], by stating that the butter in the *aupabhṛta* vessel is poured together for the sake of the subsequent *prayāja*s, its dual purpose was established.

It has been released. How is it that the suspicion arises that it serves solely the purpose of the after-offerings (*anuyāja*)? It is said: this [conclusion] holds true when this [principle] is established; otherwise, the act of bringing together would be merely a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for an invisible result (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
[Then] that would be eightfold. || 46 ||

It is heard in the scripture: "One takes eight [portions] in the *upabhṛt*. Regarding this, there is a doubt: are these two [separate] four-portioned offerings, or is this one single eight-portioned offering? Now, was it not stated in the section concerning the mixing (*samānayana*) that in order to perform two *prayāja* offerings, this single four-portioned offering is mixed together?
Thus [it is asked]: by what reasoning? The meaning is: "By this reasoning, namely, that in this way there will be a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārthatā).

That very point is now challenged: because of the hearing of the number eight. And a visible purpose for the act of bringing together (samānayana) is indeed appropriate, since the butter in the *jauhava* ladle is occupied with the earlier *āghāra* offering and the first three *prayāja* offerings.
It is brought forth for the sake of favoring that which is incapable of performing its own function; therefore,
here the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that the drawing of the cup (grahaṇa) must consist of exactly eight, because it is so stated in scripture (śrutatvāt).

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: because the numbers four and eight pertain to different objects, it cannot be maintained that one or the other is not applicable, since there is no contradiction. But how does the number eight bring about the number four in the *homa*? Because these two [portions] are each taken four times (*caturgṛhīta*) and joined together.
[The text] "for the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s" [indicates] a distribution for both purposes;

for the purpose of both is accomplished by means of the eight-fold drawing (*aṣṭagṛhaṇa*) from two four-fold portions (*caturgṛhīta*), according to the rule: "He draws eight [portions] into the *upabhṛt*. And the observation that "these two are four-fold portions" is established as before.
It occurs. The statement "the clarified butter portions are taken four times" thus becomes supported as an explanatory formula (*hetuvannigada*).
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the *Bṛhatī*.

For what purpose is this discussion (*adhikaraṇa*) included here in this definition of the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the non-instigator (*aprayojaka*)?

For neither the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) nor the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is understood from the rule (*vidhi*) itself. To this it is replied: this inquiry arises precisely from the rule. [Is it] the tree, the east...?
Is the inclusion [of the mantra] from the branch [text], or is it the inclusion of its being brought from the eastern part of the monastery?
The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the inclusion follows the designation, just as it follows the application (*viniyoga*).

The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: since this designation [of "branch"] is unavoidable by definition, it is the branch itself that is to be taken up, specifically as characterized by its location; and this is another distinction:
since the branch must necessarily be identified in both positions, this very position is the logical one.
[The rule applies] to the branch, because that is the primary element therein. || 7 ||
In this context, the taking up of the *parivāsana* or the taking up of the branch is considered, because it is not exhaustive.
What, then, is appropriate here? Both are [appropriate] for the *parivāsana*.

The root and the tip are the motivators (*prayojaka*) for both [actions], because both are designated as "branches" (*śākhā*). Now, it may be argued that two actions are heard here: "he cuts around" (*parivāsayati*) and "he makes" (*karoti*).
What follows from this? This follows: the cutting around (*parivāsana*) of the branch is the object (*karman*) [of the first action].
The upaveṣa is made from the *karoti* (the cutting tool). Therefore, the upaveṣa is not the instigator of the instrument of action. It is replied:
we have already stated that the word "branch" (*śākhā*) denotes both the root and the tip. In that context, one makes the upaveṣa from the root;
the tip, too, is employed for another purpose. Thus, both possess the status of being instigators.

To this it is replied: This would be so if the connection were "he makes the *upaveṣa* from the root. How, then, is the connection? It is "he makes the *upaveṣa* from the root. What follows if this is the case?

From this it follows: the *upaveṣa* is that which is produced from a different root [than the one used for the *parivāsana*]. Therefore, even though the term "branch" (*śākhā*) refers to both the top and the root together, it is established that the *parivāsana* (stripping) is not for the purpose of obtaining the *upaveṣa*.

Furthermore, the term "branch" (*śākhā*) is employed in other ritual functions specifically for the tip, as in the injunction: "With a branch, he drives away the calves. Therefore, because of this application, the word "branch" used here for the tip is intended for the purpose of trimming the base.

Therefore, the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) is not the motive factor (*prayojaka*). The motive has been stated. || 3 || But in the case of the carrying away, the term *juhoti* applies because of the commonality of the connection. || 10 ||

But surely this taking up [of the grass-bundle] is solely for the purpose of the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *prastara*; even though the root *harati* signifies a sacrifice and the deity is prescribed by the wording of the mantra, nevertheless this is still a rite of disposal, just like the final *prayāja*.
And in a rite of disposal, the substance does not have the status of a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*). But [it may be argued] as in the case of the final *prayāja*...

If it is argued that just as clarified butter (*ājya*) is subordinate even when it serves as a disposal (*pratipatti*), so too will the branch (*śākhā*) be subordinate here, it is not so. In this case, there is a disposal of the substance; however, in that other case, the purpose is the recollection of the deity.
It is logical that the substance (dravya) is subordinate (guṇabhāva) to the sacrifice (yāga).

But is it not the case that the final *prayāja* is not at all a disposal (*pratipatti*)? For a ritual act is a disposal only when a substance is therein disposed of. Who has said this—that a sacrifice which serves as a factor of action (*kāraka-artha*) is a disposal-act?
It is said that in some cases there is a *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) due to partial removal (*deśavirecana*), while in others there is remembrance (*smaraṇa*).

These are indeed specific purposes. Therefore, it cannot be argued as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the branch is a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*). It is replied: because the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is heard precisely in the context of disposal (*pratipatti*), its status as a subordinate element is established.

The proponent of the position (*pakṣavādī*) considers that not everything necessarily becomes primary in the act of comprehension. Whatever is heard in such a way ought to be exactly so; for instance, in the case of "one offers with the *juhū*," the *juhū* is merely subordinate (*guṇabhūta*).
To this it is replied: This would indeed be so if the word *saha* were not heard here;
but since the word *saha* is heard, it is understood that the branch possesses equal connection with the *prastara*.
Therefore, the branch is certainly also disposed of. Otherwise, there would be no equal connection.

Therefore, even in the case of the branch (*śākhā*), the meaning of the accusative case should be understood as being exactly like that of the *prastara* (grass-bundle). How then is there an instrumental case? This [instrumental] does not denote a grammatical factor (*kāraka*); rather, its purpose is to indicate association (*sahayoga*).
It has been stated that the shift in case-ending is used because association is indicated by what is well-known.
Because the throwing of the *prastara* is well-known, the remainder has been explained.

The carrying forward of the water (praṇayana) arises as being unconnected to two specific purposes;
subsequently, the two purposes are heard in the scripture, and thus one considers both to be the performers of the action without distinction. But [it may be objected]:
"He pours out the water" (apo ninayati).

Thus, the second [case-ending] is heard. The intention is that, because it is not something desired (*anīpsita*), it will function as a mere *kāraka*. To this it is replied: there is no reason for it to be undesired; for even though its purpose has been accomplished, it is indeed desired as the object to be communicated.

And when that which is desired is possible, it is not logical to resort to that which is undesired, because the latter is understood as being preceded by the former. Therefore, the pouring out is merely the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the waters whose purpose has been fulfilled in the act of mixing.
Thus it is established that [the sacrificer] is not the performer [of the action].
|| 6 || The handing over of the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa is like the throwing away [of the grass-bundle], because its purpose has been fulfilled. || 16 ||
The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the act of handing over the staff to Maitrāvaruṇa is a disposal (*pratipatti*), just like [the disposal] of the waters.

But is it not the case that, according to the rule "that person toward whom one intends [to give] by means of an action is the recipient (*sampradāna*)," its status as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*) is already established?

In the case of an action accompanied by a recipient (*saṃpradāna*), the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) of the object (*karman*) arises precisely because it produces pleasure for the recipient; it does not arise from being accomplished by another object, for that would result in the impossibility of its status as an object. How then [is it explained] in the case of:
"The staff-bearer recites the injunctions" (*daṇḍī praiṣānanvāha*)?
The intention is that such observations as these are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of what has already been established by chance regarding the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
To this, it is replied: [the Maitrāvaruṇa is] "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) because of the designation "the staff for the Maitrāvaruṇa."
And because of such observations as "he recites the *praiṣas*," this is indeed an *arthakarma* (a primary act for a purpose), not a *pratipatti* (a disposal rite).
But was it not said that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is obtained by chance? This very point is the flaw.

Because it would follow that [the rule] is merely optional (*pākṣikatva*). How then is the second [case-ending] justified? It was stated that "that which is not desired, though connected [to the action], takes the second case. That appears incorrect.
For the example given there, "he leaps over a snake" (*ahiṃ laṅghayati*), is indeed unacceptable. And thus, in the case of the *saktu* (barley meal), there is a transposition of case-endings.

It was stated that because it is something to be taken up (*upādeya*), it does not lack the status of being intended (*anīpsitatva*). It is replied: Well said; in the case of the groats (*saktu*), there is indeed a taking up for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*). But here, the taking up is not for the purpose of giving;
for one gives only what has already been taken up. Therefore, it can be maintained that this action is indeed "connected in that manner" (*tathāyukta*).
It is not what one most desires to speak, nor is it suitable for other case endings; therefore, it is well said that it is the "object as meaning" (*arthakarma*). [p.
Furthermore, the question arises whether it is merely the retention (*dhāraṇa*) that is employed here, or rather its production; this is another point of reflection.
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that there is indeed the status of being an agent of employment. This has been stated as a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).
And [the ritual] for the sake of the Soma-sacrifice is not required, because its purpose has already been fulfilled. || 20 ||

But what, then, is the distinction here between "with the remnant of the *prayāja*" and "with that which is smeared with *soma*"? Is it not the case that by the phrase "with the remnant of the *prayāja*" (*prayājaśeṣeṇa*), its purpose as being for the *prayāja* is understood; whereas by the phrase "with that which is smeared with *soma*" (*somaliptena*), its purpose as being for the ritual action (*karman*) is understood? Why [is this so]?

There is no distinction. It is said: even by the phrase "smeared with Soma," the connection with Soma is solely for the purpose of the Soma sacrifice. If that is so, then one who, based on the scriptural mention of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), considers the smeared Soma to be connected to a separate ritual action, might think it has the status of a remnant (*śeṣa*).

To this it is replied: even when there is a connection with another action, one thing cannot be understood as being subsidiary to another merely by virtue of that subsidiarity, just as one who is occupied elsewhere cannot be considered occupied elsewhere [simultaneously]. Therefore, the word "action" (karman) must be understood only through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
And by the word "yantī" (they go), the root-meaning is established as having the sense of the causative (*ṇij*) inherent within it;
otherwise, the meaning of the verbal root would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). This is what was stated: "And the direct Vedic statement..."
"Direct statement is more powerful than syntactical connection.
|| 9 || "There is no injunction regarding the agent, place, or time, because they are eternally inherent in the performance. || 23 ||

But surely, on the view that [the Veda] is merely reiterative, the sentence would result in being purposeless because it conveys no new information. We do not say that it is purposeless with respect to its application (*viniyoga*). In the context of application, the meaning of the sentence is indeed perceived as being thus connected. However, its status as something to be employed (*prayoktṛtva*) is not possible. How so?

Is it not possible? Because the collection of factors (*kārakagrāma*) is eternally present. For here a restriction is made with respect to the substance (*dravya*), not with respect to the factors; and that which is not a factor cannot possess the status of an agent (*prayoktṛ*).

It is possible. Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that this [injunction] is understood as a specific restriction regarding the application (viniyoga), and not as an operation of the agent.
To this, it is replied: if something other than the substance is understood as a factor of action (kāraka).
Therefore, as you have stated, in this case it is the substance itself that is understood as the *kāraka* (grammatical participant), because the case-ending arises from its denotation. [p.

But surely, a factor of action (*kāraka*) is employed only through its application to an action; and there is no object (*karman*) that is devoid of a factor of action. True, an object is not devoid of a factor of action; however, there is no such thing as a "factor of action" in general. For it is precisely that substance or quality which is presented by the case-ending (*vibhakti*).

That very [injunction] is the causal factor (*kāraka*). Therefore, even though it is the impeller (*prayoktṛ*) based on that application (*viniyoga*), a restriction (*niyama*) is possible. And it has been said: "An injunction (*niyoga*) follows the application (*viniyoga*), provided that such a possibility exists."
Likewise, the mention of qualities (guṇa) with respect to substances is due to their connection with the originative injunction.
It is indeed appropriate that a substance is the object of the case-endings, since it is understood as the *kāraka* (grammatical participant);
however, in cases such as "white" (*śveta*), a quality is merely a qualifier of that substance. But where there is [the word] "with the red one" (*aruṇayā*),...

The understanding [of the word] as a *kāraka* occurs precisely through its case-ending; this has already been established by the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*). Therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that because the purpose is the procurement of the substance (*dravya*), there is no intention to express the quality (*guṇa*) or the genus (*jāti*).
To this it is replied: It is true that this is for the purpose of procuring the substance; however, that very substance is devoid of those [qualities].

Since it is not possible to apprehend that [substance] as qualified by them, the apprehension of qualities and universals is established just like that of substances. And in the case of refinement (*saṃskāra*), it is because that [substance] is the primary factor.

Furthermore, what is the distinction regarding the *saṃskāra*? This is the distinction: the injunction for a *saṃskāra* is devoid of a governing context (*adhikāra*), because a *saṃskāra* exists for the sake of that which is to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*); here, it does not serve the purpose of a governing context.

The action is understood [from the context]. Therefore, there is indeed no intention to express [the action as the primary meaning]; this is the distinction from the two previous cases. To this it is replied: True, the qualification (*adhikāra*) is not directly understood; however, it is perceived through the fact that the substance is intended for the sake of the qualified person (*adhikṛta*).
What follows from that? What results from that? It follows that the substance, as characterized by the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), constitutes the qualification.

It is understood as a qualifier of the injunction; therefore, like a subordinate element (*guṇa*), it too is taken up by the very injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*), and thus it is said to be "like that. This being so, it has been demonstrated that the injunction regarding the subsidiary (*aṅga-vidhi*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
12. [Sūtra 27: Because the injunction "he sacrifices" (yajati) refers to the substance, the deity, and the action within the aggregate, as it achieves its purpose therein.
[Page b1016] What, then, are those objects of the qualification? They are sacrifice, giving, and oblation: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice."
"One desiring long life should give gold;
one desiring good fortune should offer oblations"—such are the examples. This is merely illustrative; there are others as well who [speak of] scriptural injunctions regarding desires (*kāmaśruti*).

They are connected. Furthermore, in order to dispel the doubt as to what distinction exists between sacrifice (*yāga*), giving (*dāna*), and oblation (*homa*) when they all consist essentially in relinquishment (*tyāga*), it was stated that their individual natures are now being described.

What, then, is the connection of this [re-offering] with the characteristic of "appropriation" (*upādāna*)? This is the connection: Is it that the mere holding of what has already been appropriated for the sake of hospitality is enjoined by both [offerings]; or is it the re-appropriation of what was previously offered; or is it a separate appropriation altogether, such that this [text] merely extends the ritual properties (*dharma*)?
Is this statement [intended for that specific case], or is this very same material cause common [to others as well]? There is no application elsewhere of that which is subordinate to something else—
just as there can be no operation in one place for that which is already occupied elsewhere.
Thus it has been stated. It has also been stated that the material used must follow its specific application (*viniyoga*).
Therefore, it is not logical that what was procured for the *ātithya* rite should be employed for the maintenance of the fires for the *upasad* and *agnīṣoma* rites.

Furthermore, an instruction regarding the disposal of the remains (*niriṣṭaka*) does not occur, as it would contradict the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). [This is because] it would involve figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

And [the act of] taking up [the substance] is not logically possible. In this way, even the extension of properties (*dharmātideśa*) is abandoned precisely for fear of [resorting to] figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, it is established that the common understanding alone is supported by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), and thus the common [substance] is what is to be taken up.
Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the Bṛhatī.

It was stated at the beginning of this chapter that in all cases, it is precisely the operation of *niyoga* (the mandate) that is being investigated.
Now, here it is considered whether or not the operation of the injunction (*vidhi*) can apply to a person by way of a connection with a fruit (*phala*).
If a connection between the person and the fruit is impossible, how can validity (*prāmāṇya*) be possible? Thus, [the question concerns] the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

This was considered in the *Lakṣaṇa* [section]: "Even that prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) presented there—how can it be that the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), being thus understood, establishes an injunction (*niyoga*) whose object is another action?

This is for the purpose of refuting that view; however, the present inquiry concerns the fact that an injunction (*niyoga*) cannot have itself as its own object. How so? Because [terms] such as "of whom" (*yasya*) cannot function as qualifiers of the person entitled (*adhikārin*).
Why is it impossible? Because an injunction cannot logically be related to that [person]. Why? Because [the person] is already established...

Because of the instruction [of the agent]. Just as in the statement "Devadatta cooks rice," it is understood that the person is merely indicated; it does not mean that "the rice must be cooked by the person. This is not the meaning of the words in the passage:
"He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood hears no evil report. [This is so] because of the difference in the cognition...

Because this meaning is understood from that [text], and there is no other cognition for it— this meaning being exactly as stated in the first definition— it is established that such passages are *arthavāda* (explanatory or commendatory statements).

But how, then, can a sentence be presented here as having two meanings? Even in a case where no distinction between two meanings is perceived, there must still be only a single meaning for that sentence; however, the distinction is to be understood through context and other such factors. What then, in this case, is actually understood as the distinction?
Furthermore,
the ambiguity of the expression has already been refuted in the very definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore,
because of its impossibility, this section appears to be merely a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
To this it is replied: it is exactly so; in the theory of *anvitābhidhāna*, there is indeed a single meaning.

However, since two purposes are possible here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that [the injunction] also serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). And it has been stated that the application (*upādāna*) follows the relationship. But was it not said that it follows the allocation (*viniyoga*), not the relationship?

It is not so; for it has been stated that *viniyoga* (application) is the cause of the relationship (*saṃbandha*), and yet *viniyoga* itself is not what is being relied upon here. Therefore, both are the conveyors [of the meaning], because two types of relationships are understood.
The status of substances and the like as being for the sake of man (*puruṣārtha*) is not determined by abandoning their connection with action.
To this it is replied: what was stated—that the adoption [of a substance] follows mere relationship—is incorrect;
the adoption follows the relationship established by the word, not [any other] relationship.

From the word "sārī," it is understood that the connection is solely for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). But is it not also understood as being connected with the ritual action? True, it is understood, but only as being conducive to human purpose.

Therefore, that alone is the signifier for which there is an understanding of the positive concomitance (anvaya). As for what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—that because the specific [meaning] is not understood, the sentence applies to both cases, as in "the *alambuṣā* plants are to be used"—that is intended only for the sake of non-determination when context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth are absent; it does not, however, mean that both meanings are conveyed by the word itself.
It can be understood. Here, however, the meaning is that because a specific [rule] has been mentioned, there is no lack of determination.

Now, having raised the objection that "nothing has been enjoined," the presentation of a general injunction is not intended to override [the specific rule], but rather with respect to the praise accomplished by the *sāman*; thus, there is no fault.

What, then, is the reason for the opponent's doubt? This is the reason for the doubt: namely, [the injunctions] "One performs the Agnihotra" and "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra."

And thus, there is no separate agency [of the agent], because even when there is a syntactic connection with the word "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), the connection with the oblation (*homa*) is understood. Likewise here as well in the case of "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*).

Even though there is a connection with a specific desire in the statement, "One desiring sensory power should offer curd," since the offering of curd is understood [from the context], the opponent (the pūrvapakṣin) maintains that the person alone is the motivator for the sake of human purpose. This being the position reached—

It is said: this is not correct, for here it is determined that even the *kratu* (the ritual intention) is the agent; for the *kratu* also possesses a mandate (*adhikāra*). It is not a connection between a subordinate element (*guṇa*) and a fruit (*phala*), as it requires its purposefulness (*aidamarthya*) in the substratum (*āśraya*).
Thus it has been stated. Therefore, this application— “one offers with curd for one desiring sense-power”— is indeed for the purpose of the oblation alone.
Thus alone is the human goal. As it has been said: "One performs the Agnihotra sacrifice," and "One who desires heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice."

Thus, it is logical that there is only one performer, because no other qualification is heard; therefore, the assumption of qualification applies only to the appropriator (*upādātṛ*). But here, since there are two qualifications—the obligatory (*nitya*) and the occasional (*naimittika*)—this distinction is appropriate.
But for substances that serve the purpose of an action, the consecration should be a property of the sacrifice.
In this case, however, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers the vow to have human purpose (puruṣārthatā), because it serves the purpose of sustaining life,
just like the rule "one should eat food facing the east" and the rule regarding the acceptance of gifts.
To this it is replied: This restrictive injunction does not tolerate the postulation of a separate qualification (*adhikāra*).
And the qualification for the sacrifice (*kratvadhikāra*) is present. When there is the proximity of a directly heard qualification, that which is not [directly] heard—

Therefore, it appears that the section on entitlement (*adhikāra*) exists for that very purpose through its designation. And because the connection with an enjoined person (*niyojya*) is obtained precisely through that purpose, there is no need for another entitlement. As for what was said—that it ought to be like the rules regarding acceptance of gifts and so forth—that is appropriate, since no entitlement is heard of in those cases.

In this case, however, it is shown that the opposite is true. Therefore, it is established that the restriction regarding the substance is indeed prompted by the sacrifice; that is to say, it is prompted by the qualification for the sacrifice. (Sūtra 5.1) Since no fruit is mentioned in the injunction, only the action itself would be enjoined, for that which is not expressed by the word [is not to be understood].
It would be understood. || 10 ||

In this context, injunctions devoid of a governing purpose (*adhikāra*) serve as the examples. The doubt is whether one must postulate a governing purpose for them, or whether they terminate in themselves. Now, [one might argue that] "it is fruitful..."

Regarding the term "fruitless" (*aphalam*), a doubt is heard in the Bhāṣya. It is said: apart from an entitlement (*adhikāra*), there is no fruit; thus, in the section concerning the one desiring heaven (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*), it is stated: "Therefore, the entitlement is established."
This has been demonstrated by the author who speaks thus. Otherwise, the conclusion would have been that the primacy of heaven is established.
Therefore, this is indeed an inquiry into whether there is a qualification for the action or no qualification.

What, then, is the initial position? It is that the injunction (*niyoga*), which culminates in the performance of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) according to the extent of the verbal statement, cannot possibly extend to the qualification (*adhikāra*). But surely, an injunction itself cannot be accomplished without a qualification.

[Page b1030] Or who has said that an injunction is not accomplished without an entitlement? It is an injunction for one who is entitled, but it is not from the injunction itself that the entitlement arises.

[Objection: But surely, because there is no one entitled [to perform it], the injunction (*niyoga*) cannot be carried out, and thus its comprehension would be sublated. [Response: There is no sublation whatsoever of the comprehension itself. As for those who are not entitled, they simply do not perform it;
what does that have to do with the comprehension? As the author of the *Bhāṣya* has said: "This path is secure; let him go."

Therefore, we do not see the authorization of anyone here. Even if an authorization were to be supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhriyamāṇa*), whose authorization would be supplied? For there is no [independent] injunction (*niyoga*).
The projection of two specificities is possible; furthermore, there is no evidence that a sentence is incomplete in this regard,
as in the case of "the cloth comes into being" (*paṭo bhavati*).

This is merely the sentence itself. There is also the case of "the cloth becomes red. Therefore, in sentences, the comprehension of another meaning is based solely upon the hearing of another word; it is not, however, [based on] another meaning that is not being heard.

There is the means of valid cognition known as conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). How then [is it explained] in the case of "One sacrifices *kapiñjala* birds for Spring" and "One sacrifices *kalaviṅka* birds for Summer"? It was stated therein that this is because no specific distinction is being apprehended.
But how then is it in common worldly usage, as in "the door"?
In such cases as "door" and so forth.
