Therefore, it follows that "whatever is stated [in the text], that alone is authoritative. To this, it is replied: just as a factor of action depends upon an action, so too an injunction depends upon a qualification.
We say: why? Because it is observed thus in common worldly usage, as in the sentence, "Devadatta, bring the white cow.

For in the world, speakers do not speak without having some specific [person] in mind; therefore, the optative and other suffixes (*liṅ*) must be employed with reference to Devadatta or Yajñadatta. But [one might object]: Devadatta and the like...
It is a qualification of the agent. We shall explain in the sixth [book] how it is not a qualification of the agent.
For, by virtue of the [textual] context, agency will be established; agency does not establish the context.
Therefore, that is called a partial scriptural statement (*śrutyekadeśa*). Furthermore, regarding what was stated here by the Commentator—
"In this way, a worldly ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) would result"— it was refuted [by the author] with the words, "Only a Vedic ellipsis..."
Thinking, "May we not suffer," and suspecting an obstruction, he said, "Do you see?
by way of an illustration.
All this designation appears to be inconsistent, since it is understood to be based on a specific injunction;
how then can it be non-Vedic? And if there is an intervention, how can there be an *anuṣaṅga* (syntactic connection)? As for what was also said: "Do you see him running? etc.

Thus [it is argued]. Because of the intervention of unrelated words, this is not a case of intervention at all; rather, it is said that there is an intervention only when a word is separated from the word with which it is semantically connected. To this, it is replied: we shall supply the ellipsis from the Veda itself. What is meant by this is that it is not supplied as a grammatical factor (*kāraka*).

How then? It is precisely by way of the qualified person (*adhikārin*). For in the worldly sphere, the connection with a result occurs through the status of being an agent (*kāraka*), because it depends on other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); likewise, the illustrative example is not [to be understood otherwise].

It is separated only by the intervention of a word, yet it remains connected with the appropriate word; whereas that which is separated by another sentence is truly "separated. Therefore, there is no separation in the case of supplying an elided governing term (*adhikāra-adhyāhāra*). Furthermore, the expression "Do you see? is well-said. Thus, [it refers to] that which is not being heard...
It is established that even the ritual acts (kārāṇi) possess specific entitlements.
|| 6 || That [result] is for all, because there is no distinction; it is heaven, because it is common to all. || 13.15 ||

It is established that an injunction (niyoga) is not devoid of an objective; however, it is not known by what specific objective it is characterized. Therefore, because no particular distinction is perceived, it pertains to all who have a desire for its result.

"It is connected"—this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). To this it is replied: when there is a connection with many, there is necessarily a connection with one. And if the injunction (*niyoga*) is fulfilled by means of one, there is no evidence for its connection with another qualification (*adhikāra*). [Objection: But surely, because no specific distinction is perceived, it is impossible to determine which one it is.

Thus it has been said. This is true if no distinction is perceived. But here, since [the injunction] is common to all, it is understood that the qualification belongs to the one who desires heaven alone; for when there is a general assumption, there is no cause for perceiving a specific [qualification]. This very point has been stated: "That [result] would be heaven, [as it is common] to all..."
"Because it is not distinct."
Kārṣṇājini holds that in the case of a sacrifice, the statements regarding results are auxiliary, like the subsidiary elements. || 8 || 17 ||

In those cases where no specific qualification is heard, heaven is the cause for the qualification [to perform the rite] because it is common to all; however, where explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) expressing a specific qualification are heard, a doubt arises: is heaven alone the cause for qualification here as well, or—

Or rather, that which is expressed by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is the actual entity. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that only what is understood from the injunction (*niyoga*) is logical; the explanatory passage, however, is merely an explanatory passage.

To this it is replied: it is logical that the fruit is precisely that which is stated in the *arthavāda*. Why? Because in this way, the purpose of the praise is accomplished through the praise of the object itself. But was it not said that the fact that heaven is the goal is understood from the injunction (*niyoga*)? And in a case of doubt, the determination is made by means of the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*).

It has been said: To this it is replied—True, there is no doubt; yet even certainty does not exist. Therefore, that meaning which is understood from the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) and so forth is alone the meaning of the sentence. And when the meaning of the sentence is not apprehended, [the injunction] cannot arise from the mandate (*niyoga*) alone.
Something is established. Therefore, it is well said that the very cause for entitlement (*adhikāra*) is that which is expressed by the *arthavāda*.
As for what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—that only the verbal suffix (*vibhakti*) is postulated, together with the meaning of the verbal root—
"The injunctive statement will provide the application. The intention is that one need not weary the mind by postulating a specific cause for an effect that already exists as a possibility.
|| 9 || Just as heaven is constant in the case of a rite performed for a desired object, so too is the sacrificial purpose inherent in a subsidiary element of the sacrifice. || 20 ||
This is now considered: if, moreover, the entitlement to heaven arises from the injunction itself,
and limiting conditions (*upādhi*) are postulated through the connection with other words— as in the case of "one should fetch vegetables"— what is the fault?

It may be so; indeed, there is no fault. However, it is difficult to maintain that a particular is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) because of its general application being undetermined, just as the act of fetching vegetables is [not distinct] from the act of fetching wood when they are conjoined.
10. [The fruit of] all desires [is obtained] through the desire for the auxiliary parts, because of the context. 21.

Regarding the statement, "The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices [are for] all desires," is this a restatement (anuvāda), or is it also an injunction (vidhi)? It is considered a restatement because its meaning is already established. How is it established? The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that some [desires] are established through the medium of certain subsidiaries (aṅga), while others are established directly.

[Page 1040] But surely this is heard as being connected specifically with the primary rite; how then can it be a restatement (anuvāda) dependent on the subsidiary? For even by way of the subsidiary, the primary rite is designated, just as in the case of the sacrificial post (yūpa).

To this it is replied: that which is understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, that one thing related to another is designated by that other—is established only when there is a restatement (*anuvāda*). However, the status of being understood through another means of valid cognition depends upon the restatement; thus, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Therefore, [the designation] is not...

Because of the word *apekṣā* (expectation), we consider that it is indeed an injunction (*niyoga*). In the case of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), however, because it is something to be enjoined as a distinct object, it is appropriate that it be an object of knowledge through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
|| 11 || In that regard, all [are included] without distinction. || 17 ||
Now this is considered: is there the attainment of all results at once, or is there performance according to one's desire?
Since it is heard that [the sacrifice] has all desires as its motive, there is no distinction in the performance.

The restriction is possible because of their oneness; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). But is it not the case that there is no such person as an "eligible performer" (*adhikārī*) named "one who desires all things," and due to the absence of such eligibility, the production of the fruit is impossible? It is replied:
if desire were a constituent part (*aṅga*) [of the rite], then being unarisen, its status as a constituent part would not be tenable.
The non-arising of desires is the cause for the non-production of all fruits when a single application is made. However,
in this context, since the qualification belongs to one who possesses all desires and is desirous, it does not apply to the application.

The arising of desire at the proper time is appropriate; therefore, when the cause exists, there can be no obstruction of that which is caused by it. To this it is replied: "The application [of the means] occurs as long as there is desire.
In this way, the establishment of the qualification (*adhikāra*) becomes logically consistent. For indeed...

We shall explain in the sixth [book] that there is entitlement to the fruit even for one who is free from desire (*akāmin*). But has it not been stated that at the time of performance, the arising of a desire is of no use because it is not an auxiliary factor (*anaṅga*)?

Who has said that at the time of application (*prayoga*), origination (*utpāda*) is the cause? We have already stated that the desire for all [results] simultaneously is not possible, precisely because it is understood through the context (*adhikāra*). And since simultaneous [desire] is impossible, the application of all [rites] at once is untenable. Therefore, the qualification (*adhikāra*) pertains to each individual desire. Or rather:

The commentator has stated that [the word "all"] refers to the intended desires as they have been specified; the intention is that there is no comprehension of those not specified. Therefore, the word "all" depends upon what has been specified, just as in the expression "everything was done. Thus, it is established that the performance is according to each individual desire. For this very reason...

And thus, the eligibility for even mutually contradictory results becomes established; for if they were performed simultaneously, there would be no arising of either death or life-span. Therefore, it is well said: "Or, there is the perfection of yoga."
Or rather, it is thus.

In this section, the question regarding the fruit of the *niyoga* is whether its status as an instigator (*prayojakabhāva*) is preceded by the assumption of a body, or whether it is merely the agency (*prayoktṛtva*) as heard in the scripture. Thereupon, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) [argues] that since no other cause for the assumption of a body is observed, and since animals and the like [attain their state] through other causes—

It is held that the projection of a result is preceded by the assumption of a body upon rebirth; for in the case of animals and the like, causes such as receiving gifts will be perceptible. However, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) maintains that the agency [of the sacrificer] extends only as far as is heard in the scripture. Why? Because the state of being an agent is understood solely through scriptural audition (*śruti*).
Because there is no distinction among all [the desires]. For no distinction is perceived as to whether [the fruit] occurs right here or only in the next world,
since the scriptural injunction regarding desire is common to both.

In this context, the author of the Bhāṣya, having introduced the non-perception of immediate succession, stated: "We do not apprehend [it] through perception or inference; it is understood from verbal testimony. That is incorrect, for it has already been stated that even from verbal testimony, immediate succession is not apprehended. This is the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya.

Because there is a general understanding [of the sequence] from the word, yet no specific understanding of "here" or "thereafter," the absence of another means of knowledge does not, by the word itself, subvert immediate succession; thus, the indicative mark (liṅga) has been stated.
|| 12 || [The sūtra states: "In the case of co-inherence, because the connection with the injunction is purposeful. || 19 ||

The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that in the injunction, "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," since the suffix -ktvā arises as a marker (*lakṣaṇa*) and a specific time is heard therein, the connection is for the purpose of indicating time.
Since the connection between the two verbal roots is understood through their having a common agent, this is indeed a connection between roots (*dhātusaṃbandha*).

And since that [connection] is not possible except through a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that it is precisely a relationship of primary and subordinate.
|| 13 || || If it is argued that it is for the sake of both [the primary and the subordinate], || 32 ||

Since the word *saṃsthāpya* (having completed) expresses final completion, and because the term *saṃsthā* cannot denote a relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgin*) with respect to the *Paurṇamāsī* sacrifice itself, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), the *Vaimṛdha* offering is indeed a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of both the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*Darśapūrṇamāsa*).

To this it is replied: if the word *saṃsthā* does not denote the status of being the principal (*aṅgin*) because it signifies completion, then the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) cannot possibly be the principal even on account of its context (*prakaraṇa*). Now, if...
The word *saṃsthāpya* (having concluded) intends the completion of the previously prescribed collection of constituent parts (*aṅgakalāpa*).

If this is so, then by virtue of the syntactical connection (*vākya*), the *Vaimṛdha* sacrifice is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Full Moon sacrifice. Furthermore, there is no distinction [in the case of the New Moon sacrifice] even if the injunction (*niyoga*) is one and the same, because this [Vaimṛdha] is also connected to the qualification (*adhikāra*). Therefore, it is established.
"The Vaimṛdha is a subsidiary of the Full Moon sacrifice.
|| 14 || "But since it does not arise [as a separate rite], it must be a time [for the offering], because of its connection with a specific purpose. || 36 ||

When there is a connection between two things whose status as subordinate members of a whole has already been determined, an injunction results solely in the prescription of time, because of the recognition of the action itself; therefore, the injunction has time as its purpose.
15. Regarding the matter of the time of origin, the time [of the rite] would be [the meaning] of the sentence, because that is its primary subject. 37.

Regarding the statement, "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with Soma," it was said that because no separate ritual action is enjoined there, the injunction serves only to designate the time. However, that argument is incorrect; for there is no distinction from the case of "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava. Therefore, in this case as well, by means of an injunction intended to designate the time—
It must be so; or else, the injunctive force (*niyoga*) must have the sense of an action in both cases, or a distinction must be stated.
Regarding this, some have stated that the distinction lies in being an injunction not introduced by a specific context (*anārabhyavidhāna*). But what, then, is this "not introduced"?

Is a distinction perceived through the prescription of the suffix *bhy*? This is the distinction: first of all, the prescription of two separate actions is not possible in cases such as "having sacrificed with this, one should sacrifice with that. Furthermore, in the case of a prescription not connected to a specific context (*anārabhyavidhāna*), not even a single action is under discussion. Therefore, [the distinction] is established by name.

The mention of the ritual action (*karma*) is for the purpose of determining the time. And it has been stated that even a name is meaningful when it is connected with qualities and results. In the case of the *Vājapeya*, however, because the *Vājapeya* is already under discussion, the injunction of a different ritual action is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Furthermore, the name will serve to extend the properties (*dharma*) of that [original] rite to this one.
This is according to the principle that "in another context, there is a difference of purpose. However, in the case of an injunction not connected to a specific context (*anārabhyavidhāna*),
since there is no other context, it is logical that both [the *jāti* and the *vyakti*] serve as the object of the ritual action (*karmārtha*).

It is incorrect to claim that it is a separate ritual action. As for those [schools] where this is recited within the very context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, what argument could possibly apply there? In that case, the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*)—what harm does that do to us?

Alternatively, this has already been resolved in the section concerning different recensional branches (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*), by stating that a single ritual action is recognized across all branches.
How is this avoided? It is logical that this very same scripture [is being referred to]. Let it be so;

nevertheless, we do not know whether the scripture is recognized through the meaning of the *anārabhyavāda* (uncontextualized statement), or rather through the meaning found within the specific context (*prakaraṇa*). Since there is no contradiction, recognition occurs by means of the *anārabhyavāda*; [otherwise] there would be a difference.
The learned hold this view; therefore, it is well said here that "conjunction" has the sense of a "part. Thus, the observation has been stated.
But the connection with the fruit would not apply to that which is not enjoined, because it is not something to be accomplished in its entirety. || 38 ||

In this regard, there is a doubt: does the fruit belong to him for whom there is the injunction, or does the injunction belong to one while the fruit belongs to another? Furthermore, it is the qualified person (*adhikārī*) who is enjoined. He for whose sake the ritual act is performed is the qualified person; he alone is enjoined. He for whose sake the ritual act is performed is the qualified person.
Thus he is enjoined. And if the father lacks eligibility (*anadhikāra*), he would not be subject to this injunction.

Therefore, a doubt arises: what is correct? That the fruit belongs to the father who is the one enjoined. Why? Because an injunction is for the purpose of establishing eligibility; it is not understood merely as a relationship.
Therefore, let this fruit belong to the father; let there be a connection through the praise of the succession of the son's fruit.
By means of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), it is a qualification of the person entitled [to the rite]. And thus, when the occasion connected with the sacrifice has arisen— [p.
The fruit belongs only to the one who is enjoined; it is not connected with the sacrifice itself. To this it is replied:

the fruit belongs only to that person for whom there is a connection with the fruit, because the qualification [for the rite] is established even by way of being the occasion (nimitta) for the fruit. For the other [person], there is a human purpose even through the birth of a son as the occasion.

Thus, the accomplishment of the qualification [for the rite] is established. How, then, is the word "result" (phala) to be understood? It is neither a qualifier of the ritual action (*karman*), nor does it pertain to the qualification (*adhikāra*). It is said: it will pertain to the qualification. Why?
Because such a birth of a son is heard of as a qualifier of the qualified person (*adhikārin*). Therefore, for one who...
That the fruit belongs to that very person who is enjoined is not contradictory, since the qualification for the rite is established through pleasure.
As it was stated regarding the connection with the sacrifice that the fruit belongs to the one who is enjoined, this is logical because of the qualification for the rite.
We shall explain in the sixth [chapter] that this is because of the entry into the sign (*nimitta*);
or rather, it is thus.

It is heard in the scriptures: "When a son is born. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the occasional rite (naimittika) take place immediately after birth, or does it require the inclusion of all auxiliary elements (aṅga), as is obtained by analogy with the model sacrifice (prakṛti)?
If this is so, why is the maintenance of the prince's life presented as a cause for excellence?

Let this be a single section (*adhikaraṇa*) alone; since it is contingent upon its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), its performance is not possible immediately after the occasion (*nimitta*); therefore, it must be performed at its own proper time. Nor is there [a rule of] immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction regarding its being a cause (*nimitta*), because a cause is characterized by its connection with past cognitions (*bhūtapratyaya*).
Furthermore, the state of having occurred (*bhūtatva*) does not depart at every moment of perception. Therefore, it appears that treating this as a separate topic is as good as purposeless.

To this it is replied: the general rule is that the effect follows immediately after the cause; thus, no prolongation of time is understood to occur without a cause. But has not the cause already been stated?

The status of the subsidiary (aṅga) as being occasional (naimittika) is precisely this: we do not know whether, because the injunction (niyoga) is understood at the time of the occasion, the subsidiary—whose application (viniyoga) is understood through the ritual connection—should be abandoned; or rather, whether the time of the injunction itself should be postponed. Since the application exists for the sake of the injunction, the abandonment of the subsidiary [follows from that].

The learned authorities hold this view: just as the prescribed time, such as the forenoon, is disregarded by touching someone who is menstruating or otherwise impure, so too is the preceding section intended to override that [rule]. For if the performance were carried out only at the time of the formal injunction (*niyoga*), then that very purpose for which the injunction exists would be lost.

Therefore, it is only the comprehension of the time for the injunction that should be postponed. And if it is postponed, it would occur at its own proper time; thus, there is no authority for abandoning the auxiliary elements—this is the second section.
Written.
|| 17 || Because of the connection with the primary [act], the subsidiary parts share the time of the principal. || 40 ||

Regarding the statement, “Having performed the Vājapeya sacrifice, one should perform the Bṛhaspatisava,” there arises a doubt: is there a single injunction (niyoga), or are there two injunctions? Now, [one might object]:...

If there were two independent injunctions (*niyoga*), the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) would not be possible; yet such a relationship of principal and subordinate does exist.
Therefore, there is no difference in performance (*prayogabheda*). Certainly it is possible; the status of principal and subordinate arises from the application (*viniyoga*).

Due to the difference in application (*prayoga*), there is a difference in ritual employment (*viniyoga*). But surely, if there were a difference in injunction (*niyoga*), it would follow that there is a division of the scripture (*śāstra*). Let it be so in view of the application; there is no fault whatsoever. However, in view of the ritual employment, this scripture is indeed one and the same. But how can there be a difference in application if the scripture is a single unity?
By what can that which is caused by a connection [of subsidiaries] be prevented from being like a difference in procedure?

In whatever way something is connected, in that very way it differentiates the *tantra*. Here, however, because of the difference in the connection of the performance (*prayoga*), a difference in performance results. Let there be no fault with respect to this difference in performance.
Therefore, there is no transition to another scripture; there is merely a difference in ritual application (*prayoga*). How this difference in application occurs has been demonstrated.
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Bṛhatī*.
The fourth quarter of the fourth chapter.
1. Because of the commonality of the term "section" (prakaraṇa), there is no status as a subsidiary part for the injunctions.

But surely, in the discussion on names, it was stated that something becomes a name because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). How, then, can it be suspected that this [term] denotes even that which has no connection to the meaning of sacrificing?
Therefore, this prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is untenable. It is replied: In this case, however—

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that because the injunction is one, there is a simultaneous denotation of the root-meanings; and since the unity of the injunction depends upon the context (prakaraṇa), the verbal root denotes all the actions under discussion.

This being the case, it is replied: It is true that there is a unity of injunction (*niyoga*) due to the context; however, this does not constitute a reason for abandoning the connection with what is heard [in the text]. Why? Because even the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) does not at all contradict the unity of the injunction. We shall explain this under the heading "because of the instruction of such a state."
Therefore, it is established that the subsidiary (aṅga) is distinct from the sacrifice. That which is situated in the middle belongs to that [sacrifice] which is in the middle.

But is it not the case that here too, the principle that "context is stronger than sequence" has already been illustrated? And the fact that [the *prastara-homa*] applies to all [offerings] was established in the third [book]. It is replied: True, it is established by virtue of its application (*viniyoga*).

But now, because the application (*niyoga*) of the consecration (*abhiṣecanīya*) rite is to be performed separately and because it is in close proximity (*sannidhāna*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that its unity with that [consecration] alone is appropriate. There is no contradiction with the application; for the context (*prakaraṇa*) is the cause for the connection with each [individual element]. Therefore, due to proximity—

The transcendence of the specific [application] is not tenable. To this it is replied: the principle of "single-wordness" (*ekaśabdya*) is established for the governing injunction (*adhikāravidhi*). What follows from that? This follows from it: only for that which has a distinction in its connection with the performance (*prayogānubandhabheda*) is a separate performance determined by its own procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

According to Kālāpa: furthermore, for that constituent part whose performance is indicated solely by the injunction of entitlement (*adhikāravidhi*), an intermediate performance (*avāntaraprayoga*) cannot be indicated. Therefore, the performance of that very constituent at its [prescribed] place, as understood from the injunction of entitlement, is established precisely through the sequence (*krama*).
[1060] You yourself have stated that there is no contradiction with the context. || 3 || Furthermore, if the context were not divided, both [positions] would indeed be contradictory. || 5 ||

"Before the Upasads, they proceed with the Saumya [offering]," it is said. "But what indeed is the distinction of those who proceed with the Anuyājas after the Āgnimāruta?"—there is indeed no distinction.
Why then is there another section for the Saumya and others, rather than another section? What to us...?
Is there a contradiction? Indeed, there is no contradiction for you. However, there is the pointlessness of the *adhikaraṇa* (the formal discussion).

In that case, this is the distinction: according to the context (*prakaraṇa*), everything in the *Rājasūya* would possess either predominance or the status of being a procedure (*itikartavyatā*). And it has been stated that "that which is not connected [by direct statement] is [determined] by context."
Therefore, the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that [the rite] is indeed a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the *upasads* because of that sentence. Moreover,
it is logical that it is a subsidiary of the *upasads* precisely due to the specific proximity (*sannidhāna*), because of the governing injunction (*adhikāraniyoga*).

To this it is replied: first of all, there is no *prakaraṇa* (contextual setting) for the *upasads*, because a *prakaraṇa* is established by way of a governing injunction (*adhikāra*). Now, it was argued that [the connection] with the *upasads* arises from syntactical connection (*vākya*);
however, a syntactical connection is not possible here because there is no relation between the two words. Therefore...

The connection is indeed "prior to the Upasads. Now, why is it that the connection "of the Upasads with the Saumya" does not occur? For in that case, the word "prior to" (purastāt) would result in being syntactically disconnected (ananvaya).
Since the connection with "purastāt" (before) is a prescription of time, the statement "they proceed with the Soma sacrifice" is not contradictory.
Therefore, this [rule] also is no different from the rule regarding that which follows the Āgnimāruta [offering].
Or rather, because of the stated reason, the other would be the primary [act], as it possesses a fruit. (Sūtra 7)

However, although it is already established by the principle that "in the vicinity of that which possesses a fruit, that which lacks a fruit is its subsidiary" (*sāṅgrahaṇī*)—as in the case of the *Sāṅgrahaṇī* sacrifice—this section is intended to preclude the application of *anuṣaṅga* (automatic extension). And this has been demonstrated.
|| 5 || 1. The *dadhi-graha* is occasional (*naimittika*), because of its connection with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). || 8 ||

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers [the act] to be occasional (naimittika), because it is proclaimed for the purpose of removing the defect of impermanence. The teacher-like one (ācāryadeśīya) maintains that it serves both purposes, like the *khadira* wood. He holds that the application of the term "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) is justified only if [the act] is permanent (*nitya*). However, the final conclusion (rāddhānta) is that this is not so, due to the absence of a connection with an occasioning condition (*nimitta*).
It cannot be assumed that this [practice] is occasional (naimittika) merely for the purpose of removing a fault.
Why can it not be so assumed? Because the removal of an occasional fault would otherwise be inexplicable, it must itself be occasional. True, if it were otherwise.
It is not tenable; however, as a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), it is indeed tenable, and thus does not require further conceptualization.
It is logical on account of its similarity (*sārūpya*).
And Vaiśvānara must be eternal, because he possesses the same number as the eternal [fires].

If it should be argued that this is also possible by way of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for the purpose of removing the defect of impermanence—such that even in the case of Vaiśvānara there would be permanence—this is the conceit of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). But is it not the case that, without a single injunction (*niyoga*), the state of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatā*) is simply impossible? True, it would be impossible; however, the state of having a common agent is established by virtue of the unity of the qualification (*adhikāra*).

And as for the objection that there is no recognition of the subject matter at hand because of hearing the word *darśa*, that has been refuted by the observation of a single meaning in the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*). The author of the Bhāṣya stated, "In this way, there is a primary proximity," and having raised the objection regarding similarity with the *saurya* and other [offerings], he further presented the point of dissimilarity; what is that?

that which is called "commencement" (pravṛtti) is an undertaking that is independent of sequence; and if an undertaking is independent, it has already commenced.
For one who thinks that there is a purpose for the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even when there is further dependence, this is the reply:
the proximity to the principal [element] understood from the simultaneous injunction becomes impaired by inequality;
however, in the case of equality, it remains exactly as authorized. For the sake of establishing that:

A restrictive rule (niyama) must be accepted; and since that rule is preceded by an initial application, it is explained by that very [initial application]. Now, for what purpose is the observation of the *saurya* sacrifice and others?

If sequence is respected merely because it is perceived in succession, then what aversion could there be toward [the sequence] in the *saurya* and other such rites? Indeed, none at all. However, even if it is perceived, it is abandoned because it is not useful for performance—just as the individual form of the phonemes (*varṇa*) is abandoned within words (*pada*), or unity is abandoned within sentences (*vākya*), or [the distinction between] the cups (*graha*) is abandoned.

Just as in the case of sacrificial oblations where there is a dual nature, the abandonment of even that which is suitable is not justified by this alone. Therefore, what is required is respected when it is obtained; yet, even if obtained, that which is not required—
It must indeed be regarded as such. But if this is so, does it not follow that the act of comprehension (*pratipatti*) becomes purposeless? Who has said that comprehension is purposeless?

It is precisely a purposeful comprehension that is the cause of purposefulness, not mere comprehension, nor non-comprehension; for comprehension culminates in [the realization of] the object. Thus it has been well said.

In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya has cited the example, "He sacrifices the animals together," thinking that it is not within the scope [of the argument], because the sequence of the traditional recitation (*samāmnāya-krama*), though existing in cases such as the Triṇava and others, is not observed there. Thus, considering it to be outside the scope, he has cited this.

And here, having taken up the matter established in another section— namely, that "one sacrifices the animals together"— and it being settled that this simultaneity applies to the place of the *savanīya* animal, what is the rule for the sequence?

Thus it is considered: is the sequence here also caused solely by the order of occurrence (*pravṛtti*), or is there another cause? In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) argues that since a sequence is necessarily present, if the order of occurrence were not accepted as the cause, then the restriction would follow simply from the previously understood textual recitation (*pāṭha*).

[The opponent] thinks thus. But the proponent of the final view (rāddhāntavādī), stating that the position is not sublated by the mention of "together," has declared that it is logical for the *savanīya* offering itself to be performed first.
If this is so, what is the status of the Agniṣomīya and the Anubandhya? How is there a sequence here?

What is the use of this irrelevant inquiry? Or rather, since it is improper to override the time [of the Savanīya] on account of its position, the Agniṣomīya alone should come first. If that is the case, then [the same would apply] even to the Savanīya.

If this is so, then this is a consideration of relative strength (*balābala*), not a restriction [of the means of knowledge] based on the nature of the object.

Herein lies the consideration of relative strength (*balābalacintā*). The position of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) is that since the sequence is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*) and because the comprehension [of the order] is equal, there is an option (*vikalpa*). The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that because it contradicts what is to be enjoined, the comprehension itself is unequal; thus, the relative strength belongs only to the direct statement (*śruti*) and the meaning (*artha*).

In this case, when there is a conflict between the literal sense (*śruti*) and the purpose (*artha*), how is it? There is no such example at all; rather, the purpose alone is more powerful. For here, by the word "purpose" (*artha*), the "task" (*kārya*) is meant, and the sequence is for the sake of that task. Therefore...
It subverts the scriptural text, because that [text] has the ritual action as its object.
Regarding the portions, the sprinkling, and the placing, the sequence should be determined by the order of performance.

Here too, the consideration is precisely one of relative strength (*balābala*). The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that because the sequence of performance (*pravṛtti*) occurs first, it is stronger. The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that because the order is for the sake of the ritual action (*kārya*) and because the act of cutting (*avadāna*) is the commencement of the offering (*pradāna*), the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*) is stronger. As for the phrase "having performed the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices," its establishment [as a requirement] follows from its being an injunction of time. To this, it is replied:
this present-tense suffix does not [function] except as indicating immediate succession to the *ādhāna*.

But where is this not possible? In the case of the qualification (adhikāra). And the injunction is dependent upon that qualification.
Thus, even in the injunction for the establishment of the fires (ādhāna), the sequence is implied by implication; this has been shown as a further argument.
